The **usage share of an operating system** is the percentage of [computers](/wiki/Computer "Computer") running that [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") (OS). These statistics are estimates as usage data is difficult to obtain and measure.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Reliable primary sources are limited and data collection methodology is not formally agreed upon.

Devices connecting to the [World Wide Web](/wiki/World_Wide_Web "World Wide Web") log which operating system they're using, and so are an approximate measure of OS usage among consumer devices. As of December 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Usage_share_of_operating_systems&action=edit), among all devices [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)"), which uses the [Linux kernel](/wiki/Linux_kernel "Linux kernel"), is the world's most common operating system to connect to the [web](/wiki/World_Wide_Web "World Wide Web") with 34.9% of the global market, followed by [Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") with 29.98%, [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS") with 16.81%, [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") with 2.03%, and other operating systems with 9.06% total.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Between different classes of devices:
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Usage share of operating systems

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
- For smartphones and other mobile devices, Android has 72% share of traffic, and Apple's iOS has 28%.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
- For desktop computers and laptops, Microsoft Windows has 62.16%, followed by unknown operating systems at 18.75%, Mac OS at 14.58%, [desktop Linux](/wiki/Desktop_Linux "Desktop Linux") at 3.09%, then Google's [ChromeOS](/wiki/ChromeOS "ChromeOS") at 1.42%, as of June 2026.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)
- For tablets, Apple's [iPadOS](/wiki/IPadOS "IPadOS") (a variant of iOS) has 51.23% share and Android has 48.61% worldwide.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Of the [top 500](/wiki/TOP500 "TOP500") most powerful [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer"), all since November 2017 have used [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux"). [[8]](#cite_note-8)

The global server operating system market share has Linux leading with a 63.1% market share, followed by Windows, [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") and other operating systems.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
The global server operating system market share has Linux leading with a 63.1% market share, followed by Windows, [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") and other operating systems.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The most numerous type of device with an operating system are [embedded systems](/wiki/Embedded_system "Embedded system"). Not all embedded systems have operating systems, instead running their application code on the "bare metal"; of those that do have operating systems, a high percentage are standalone or do not have a web browser, which makes their usage share difficult to measure. Some operating systems used in embedded systems are more widely used than some of those mentioned above. For example, modern Intel microprocessors contain an [embedded management processor](/wiki/Intel_Management_Engine "Intel Management Engine") running a version of the [Minix](/wiki/Minix "Minix") operating system.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

On 27 January 2016, Paul Thurrott summarized the operating system market, the day after Apple announced "one billion devices":

> Apple's "active installed base" is now one billion devices. [..] Granted, some of those Apple devices were probably sold into the marketplace years ago. But that 1 billion figure can and should be compared to the numbers Microsoft touts for Windows 10 (200 million, most recently) or Windows more generally (1.5 billion active users, a number that hasn’t moved, magically, in years), and that Google touts for Android (over 1.4 billion, as of September).
> My understanding of iOS is that the user base was previously thought to be around 800 million strong, and when you factor out Macs and other non-iOS Apple devices, that's probably about right. But as you can see, there are three big personal computing platforms. And only one of them is actually declining. We’ll see how Windows 10 fares over the long term, but even if Microsoft hits the 1 billion figure in 1-2 years as promised, it will by then still be the smallest of those three platforms.

### PC shipments

For 2015 (and earlier), Gartner reports for "the year, worldwide PC shipments declined for the fourth consecutive year, which started in 2012 with the launch of tablets" with an 8% decline in PC sales for 2015 (not including cumulative decline in sales over the previous years).[[24]](#cite_note-Sales15-24)

Microsoft backed away from their goal of one billion Windows 10 devices in three years (or "by the middle of 2018")[[25]](#cite_note-25) and reported on 26 September 2016 that Windows 10 was running on over 400 million devices,[[26]](#cite_note-26) and in March 2019, on more than 800 million.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

title: Usage share of operating systems

Microsoft backed away from their goal of one billion Windows 10 devices in three years (or "by the middle of 2018")[[25]](#cite_note-25) and reported on 26 September 2016 that Windows 10 was running on over 400 million devices,[[26]](#cite_note-26) and in March 2019, on more than 800 million.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In May 2020, [Gartner](/wiki/Gartner "Gartner") predicted further decline in all market segments for 2020 due to [COVID-19](/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), predicting a decline of 13.6% for all devices. while the "Work from Home Trend Saved PC Market from Collapse", with only a decline of 10.5% predicted for PCs. However, in the end, according to Gartner, PC shipments grew 10.7% in the fourth quarter of 2020 and reached 275 million units in 2020, a 4.8% increase from 2019 and the highest growth in ten years." Apple in 4th place for PCs had the largest growth in shipments for a company in Q4 of 31.3%, while "the fourth quarter of 2020 was another remarkable period of growth for Chromebooks, with shipments increasing around 200% year over year to reach 11.7 million units. In 2020, Chromebook shipments increased over 80% to total nearly 30 million units, largely due to demand from the North American education market." Chromebooks sold more (30 million) than Apple's Macs worldwide (22.5 million) in pandemic year 2020.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In 2024 and 2025, due to lower adoption of [Windows 11](/wiki/Windows_11 "Windows 11") and Microsoft ending its support to [Windows 10](/wiki/Windows_10 "Windows 10"),[[31]](#cite_note-31) the number of PCs shipped with [pre-installed](/wiki/Pre-installed_software "Pre-installed software") Windows OS dropped. Pundits attribute the low Windows 11 acceptance to its steep hardware requirements and especially the TPM 2.0 ready chipset requirement[[32]](#cite_note-32) and the [2024 CrowdStrike-related IT outages](/wiki/2024_CrowdStrike-related_IT_outages "2024 CrowdStrike-related IT outages").[[33]](#cite_note-33) Meanwhile, the macOS device market share in PC device shipments increased to new heights,[[34]](#cite_note-34) with improved numbers seen for Linux devices too.[[35]](#cite_note-35) In Q3 2025, the macOS pre-installed device shipments increased by 14.9% [year-over-year](/wiki/Year-over-year "Year-over-year") (YoY), while the overall PC-shipments increased only by 8.1%,[[36]](#cite_note-36) in Q2 2025, it grew 21.4% YoY while the global PC-shipments increased only by 6.5%,[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38) and in Q1 2025, it grew 7% YoY while the global PC-shipments increased by 4.8%.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

In 2015, [eMarketer](/wiki/EMarketer "EMarketer") estimated at the beginning of the year that the tablet [installed base](/wiki/Installed_base "Installed base") would hit one billion[[40]](#cite_note-40) for the first time (with China's use at 328 million, which [Google Play](/wiki/Google_Play "Google Play") doesn't serve or track, and the United States's use second at 156 million). At the end of the year, because of cheap tablets – not counted by all analysts – that goal was met (even excluding cumulative sales of previous years) as:

> Sales quintupled to an expected 1 billion units worldwide this year, from 216 million units in 2014, according to projections from the Envisioneering Group. >
> While that number is far higher than the 200-plus million units globally projected by research firms IDC, Gartner and Forrester, Envisioneering analyst Richard Doherty says the rival estimates miss all the cheap Asian knockoff tablets that have been churning off assembly lines.[..]
>
> Forrester says its definition of tablets "is relatively narrow" while IDC says it includes some tablets by Amazon — but not all.[..]
>
> The top tech purchase of the year continued to be the smartphone, with an expected 1.5 billion sold worldwide, according to projections from researcher IDC. Last year saw some 1.2 billion sold.[..]
>
> Computers didn’t fare as well, despite the introduction of Microsoft's latest software upgrade, Windows 10, and the expected but not realized bump it would provide for consumers looking to skip the upgrade and just get a new computer instead. >
> Some 281 million PCs were expected to be sold, according to IDC, down from 308 million in 2014. Folks tend to be happy with the older computers and keep them for longer, as more of our daily computing activities have moved to the smartphone.[..]
>
> While Windows 10 got good reviews from tech critics, only 11% of the 1-billion-plus Windows user base opted to do the upgrade, according to Microsoft. This suggests Microsoft has a ways to go before the software gets "hit" status.

### Smartphone shipments

There are more mobile phone owners than toothbrush owners,[[50]](#cite_note-51) with mobile phones the fastest growing technology in history.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] There are a billion more active mobile phones in the world than people (and many more than 10 billion sold so far with less than half still in use), explained by the fact that some people have more than one, such as an extra for work.[[51]](#cite_note-52) All the phones have an operating system, but not all of them are smartphones with an OS capable of running modern applications. In 2018, 3.1 billion smartphones and tablets were in use across the world (with tablets, a small fraction of the total, generally running the same operating systems, Android or iOS, the latter being more popular on tablets. In 2019, a variant of iOS called [iPadOS](/wiki/IPadOS "IPadOS") built for iPad tablets was released).

On 28 May 2015, Google announced that there were 1.4 billion Android users and 1 billion Google play users active during that month.[[52]](#cite_note-53)[[53]](#cite_note-54) This changed to 2 billion monthly active users in May 2017.[[54]](#cite_note-55)[[55]](#cite_note-56)

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
On 28 May 2015, Google announced that there were 1.4 billion Android users and 1 billion Google play users active during that month.[[52]](#cite_note-53)[[53]](#cite_note-54) This changed to 2 billion monthly active users in May 2017.[[54]](#cite_note-55)[[55]](#cite_note-56)

By late 2016, Android had been said to be "killing" Apple's iOS market share (i.e. its declining sales of smartphones, not just relatively but also by number of units, when the whole market was increasing).[[56]](#cite_note-57) Gartner's press release stated: "Apple continued its downward trend with a decline of 7.7 percent in the second quarter of 2016",[[57]](#cite_note-58) which is their decline, based on absolute number of units, that underestimates the relative decline (with the market increasing), along with the misleading "1.7 [percent [point]](/wiki/Percentage_point "Percentage point")" decline. That point decline means an 11.6% relative decline (from 14.6% down to 12.9%).

Although by units sold Apple was declining in the late 2010s, the company was almost the only vendor making any profit in the smartphone sector from hardware sales alone. In Q3 2016 for example, they captured 103.6% of the market profits.[[58]](#cite_note-59)

In May 2019, the biggest smartphone companies (by market share) were Samsung, Huawei and Apple, respectively.[[59]](#cite_note-60)

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
Although by units sold Apple was declining in the late 2010s, the company was almost the only vendor making any profit in the smartphone sector from hardware sales alone. In Q3 2016 for example, they captured 103.6% of the market profits.[[58]](#cite_note-59)

In May 2019, the biggest smartphone companies (by market share) were Samsung, Huawei and Apple, respectively.[[59]](#cite_note-60)

In November 2024, a new competitor to Android and iOS emerged, when sales of the Huawei [Mate 70](/wiki/Huawei_Mate_70 "Huawei Mate 70") started with the all-new operating system [HarmonyOS NEXT](/wiki/HarmonyOS_NEXT "HarmonyOS NEXT") installed[[60]](#cite_note-61) on the flagship device. Since 2025 all new Huawei devices have exclusively been sold with the HarmonyOS NEXT operating system, creating a third player on the market for smartphone operating systems.[[61]](#cite_note-62)[[62]](#cite_note-63)

In the first quarter of 2025, Huawei, which at that time almost exclusively sold smartphones with its HarmonyOS NEXT operating system, overtook Chinese company [Xiaomi](/wiki/Xiaomi "Xiaomi") to become the best-selling smartphone brand in China, with a 19 per cent market share.[[63]](#cite_note-64)

Rising RAM prices at the end of 2025 caused Gartner to predict reduction in both PC and smartphone sales.[[64]](#cite_note-65) That prediction was proven right for the first quarter of 2026.[[65]](#cite_note-66)

Android currently ranks highest,[[94]](#cite_note-AndroWin-95) above Windows (incl. Xbox console) systems. [Windows Phone](/wiki/Windows_Phone "Windows Phone") accounted for 0.51% of the web usage, before it was discontinued.[[95]](#cite_note-96)

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
Android currently ranks highest,[[94]](#cite_note-AndroWin-95) above Windows (incl. Xbox console) systems. [Windows Phone](/wiki/Windows_Phone "Windows Phone") accounted for 0.51% of the web usage, before it was discontinued.[[95]](#cite_note-96)

Considering all personal computers, [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") is well below 50% usage share on every continent, and at 30% in the US (24% single-day low) and in many countries lower, e.g. China, and in India at 19% (12% some days) and Windows' lowest share globally was 29% in May 2022 (25% some days), and 29% in the US.[[96]](#cite_note-97)

For a short time, iOS was slightly more popular than Windows in the US, but this is no longer the case. Worldwide, Android holds 45.49%, more than Windows at 25.35%, and iOS third at 18.26%.

In Africa, Android is at 53.17%, Windows is 21.53 (and iOS third at 9.71%).[[97]](#cite_note-98)

Before iOS became the most popular operating system in any independent country, it was most popular in Guam, an [unincorporated territory of the United States](/wiki/Unincorporated_territories_of_the_United_States "Unincorporated territories of the United States"), for four consecutive quarters in 2017–18,[[98]](#cite_note-99)[[99]](#cite_note-100) although Android is now the most popular there.[[100]](#cite_note-101) iOS has been the highest ranked OS in [Jersey](/wiki/Jersey "Jersey") (a British [Crown dependency](/wiki/Crown_dependencies "Crown dependencies") in Europe) for years, by a wide margin, and iOS was also highest ranked in Falkland Islands, a [British Overseas Territory](/wiki/British_Overseas_Territories "British Overseas Territories"), for one quarter in 2019, before being overtaken by Android in the following quarter.[[101]](#cite_note-102)[[102]](#cite_note-103) iOS is competitive with Windows in Sweden, where some days it is more used.[[103]](#cite_note-104)

The designation of an "Unknown" operating system is strangely high in a few countries such as [Madagascar](/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar") where it was at 32.44% (no longer near as high).[[104]](#cite_note-105) This may be due to the fact that StatCounter uses [browser detection](/wiki/Browser_detection "Browser detection") to get OS statistics, and there the most common browsers are not often used. The version breakdown for browsers in Madagascar shows "Other" at 34.9%,[[105]](#cite_note-106) and [Opera Mini](/wiki/Opera_Mini "Opera Mini") 4.4 is the most popular known browser at 22.1% (plus e.g. 3.34% for Opera 7.6). However browser statistics without version-breakdown has Opera at 48.11% with the "Other" category very small.[[106]](#cite_note-107)[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*]

In China, Android became the highest ranked operating system in July 2016 (Windows has occasionally topped it since then, while since April 2016 it or all non-mobile operating systems haven't outranked mobile operating systems, meaning Android plus iOS).[[107]](#cite_note-108) In the Asian continent as a whole, Android has been ranked highest since February 2016 and Android alone has the majority share,[[108]](#cite_note-109) because of a large majority in all the most populous countries of the continent, up to 84% in Bangladesh, where it has had over 70% share for over four years.[[109]](#cite_note-Bangladesh-110) Since August 2015, Android is ranked first, at 48.36% in May 2016, in the African continent – when it took a big jump ahead of Windows 7,[[110]](#cite_note-111) and thereby Africa joined Asia as a mobile-majority continent. China is no longer a desktop-majority country,[[111]](#cite_note-112) joining India, which has a mobile-majority of 71%, confirming Asia's significant mobile-majority.

StatCounter's OS X and macOS numbers are combined as macOS. Percentages may not add up to 100% due to rounding. | | | | |

Windows is still the dominant desktop OS, but the dominance varies by region and it has gradually lost market share to other desktop operating systems (not just to mobile) with the slide very noticeable in the US, where macOS usage has more than quadrupled from Jan. 2009 to Dec. 2020 to 30.62% (i.e., in Christmas month; and 34.72% in April 2020 in the middle of [COVID-19](/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), and iOS was more popular overall that year;[[127]](#cite_note-129) globally Windows lost to Android that year,[[128]](#cite_note-130) as for the two years prior), with Windows down to 61.136% and ChromeOS at 5.46%, plus traditional Linux at 1.73%.[[129]](#cite_note-131) As of March 2025, Windows holds 71.68% of the global desktop OS market share, macOS 15.7%, Linux (excluding ChromeOS) 4.20%, and ChromeOS 1.86%. In the US, as of March 2025, Windows has 54.38%, macOS 28.53%, Linux (excluding ChromeOS) 6.42%, and ChromeOS 8.44%.

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
Windows is still the dominant desktop OS, but the dominance varies by region and it has gradually lost market share to other desktop operating systems (not just to mobile) with the slide very noticeable in the US, where macOS usage has more than quadrupled from Jan. 2009 to Dec. 2020 to 30.62% (i.e., in Christmas month; and 34.72% in April 2020 in the middle of [COVID-19](/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), and iOS was more popular overall that year;[[127]](#cite_note-129) globally Windows lost to Android that year,[[128]](#cite_note-130) as for the two years prior), with Windows down to 61.136% and ChromeOS at 5.46%, plus traditional Linux at 1.73%.[[129]](#cite_note-131) As of March 2025, Windows holds 71.68% of the global desktop OS market share, macOS 15.7%, Linux (excluding ChromeOS) 4.20%, and ChromeOS 1.86%. In the US, as of March 2025, Windows has 54.38%, macOS 28.53%, Linux (excluding ChromeOS) 6.42%, and ChromeOS 8.44%.

There is little openly published information on the device shipments of desktop and laptop computers. Gartner publishes estimates, but the way the estimates are calculated is not openly published. Another source of market share of various operating systems is [StatCounter](/wiki/StatCounter "StatCounter")[[130]](#cite_note-132) basing its estimate on web use (although this may not be [very accurate](/wiki/Usage_share_of_web_browsers#Accuracy "Usage share of web browsers")). Also, sales may overstate usage. Most computers are sold with a [pre-installed operating system](/wiki/Pre-installed_software "Pre-installed software"), with some users replacing that OS with a different one due to personal preference, or installing another OS alongside it and using both. Conversely, sales underestimate usage by not counting unauthorized copies. For example, in 2009, approximately 80% of software sold in China consisted of illegitimate copies.[[131]](#cite_note-133) In 2007, the statistics from an automated update of IE7 for registered Windows computers differed with the observed web browser share, leading one writer to estimate that 25–35% of all Windows XP installations were unlicensed.[[132]](#cite_note-134)

The usage share of Microsoft's (then latest operating system version) [Windows 10](/wiki/Windows_10 "Windows 10") has slowly increased since July/August 2016, reaching around 27.15% (of all Windows versions, not all desktop or all operating systems) in December 2016. It eventually reached 79.79% on 5 October 2021, the same day on which its successor [Windows 11](/wiki/Windows_11 "Windows 11") was released. StatCounter web usage data of desktop or laptop operating systems varies significantly by country. For example, in 2017, macOS usage in North America was at 16.82%[[134]](#cite_note-136) (17.52% in the US[[135]](#cite_note-137)) whereas in Asia it was only 4.4%.[[136]](#cite_note-138) As of July 2023, macOS usage has increased to 30.81% in North America[[137]](#cite_note-139) (31.77% in the US)[[138]](#cite_note-140) and to 9.64% in Asia.[[139]](#cite_note-141)

Since mid-2020, the world uses smartphones more than desktop (including laptop) computers.[[140]](#cite_note-142)[[141]](#cite_note-143)[[142]](#cite_note-144) For global statistics it's every day of the week. It has also happened for all individual continents[[143]](#cite_note-145)[[144]](#cite_note-146)[[145]](#cite_note-147) (at least for some weeks, and also for the United States where the smartphone share reached 54.26% in July 2022,[[146]](#cite_note-148)[[147]](#cite_note-149)[[148]](#cite_note-150)[[149]](#cite_note-151) and also that high in 2021). The proportions do vary widely by region (more so than by the day), e.g. in Africa the smartphone share is highest at 72%, in Asia at 69% and in South America at 60%, in Europe is 49% while desktop is slightly lower, and in the United States it's at 43% and desktop at 54% (previously at 50%). On some continents, e.g. North America and the US, smartphone use may only go over 50% on weekends, since smartphones usage increases on weekends,[[150]](#cite_note-152)[[151]](#cite_note-153)[[152]](#cite_note-154)[[153]](#cite_note-155) while the smartphone share has gone up to 54% for a single day ([Thanksgiving](/wiki/Thanksgiving "Thanksgiving")), and on average over 50% for full week.[[154]](#cite_note-156)[[155]](#cite_note-157)

### Microsoft data on Windows usage

In June 2016, Microsoft claimed Windows 10 had half the market share of all Windows installations in the US and UK, as quoted by BetaNews:

> Microsoft's Windows trends page [shows] Windows 10 hit 50 percent in the US (51 percent in the UK, 39 percent globally), while ... Windows 7 was on 38 percent (36 percent in the UK, 46 percent globally).
> A big reason for the difference in numbers comes down to how they are recorded. ... actual OS usage (based on web browsing), while Microsoft records the number of devices Windows 10 is installed on. ... Microsoft also only records Windows 7, Windows 8, Windows 8.1 and Windows 10, while NetMarketShare includes both XP and Vista.

— BetaNews[[158]](#cite_note-160)

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
### Desktop computer games

Linux has gained more interest among gamers in the early 2020s, especially thanks to projects like [Wine](/wiki/Wine_(software) "Wine (software)") and [Proton](/wiki/Proton_(software) "Proton (software)"). Wine allows Windows programs to run on Linux, while Valve's Proton makes many games on Steam directly playable without any additional configuration. The Linux version of Steam and devices such as [Steam Deck](/wiki/Steam_Deck "Steam Deck") using Linux-based [SteamOS](/wiki/SteamOS "SteamOS") have made Linux more accessible as a gaming platform. The number of Steam games currently available on Linux exceeds the total number of games available on [XBOX](/wiki/Xbox "Xbox"), [Nintendo Switch](/wiki/Nintendo_Switch "Nintendo Switch") and [PlayStation](/wiki/PlayStation "PlayStation") platforms.[[159]](#cite_note-161) In addition, on modern systems, Linux is able to offer comparable or sometimes higher performance than Windows in some games due to its lower system load.[[160]](#cite_note-162) These developments have made Linux a more viable alternative to Windows in terms of game playability compared to the past.

The digital video game distribution platform [Steam](/wiki/Steam_(service) "Steam (service)") publishes data monthly through their [Hardware & Software Survey](https://store.steampowered.com/hwsurvey/):

### Smartphones OS by usage

See also: [Mobile operating system § Market share](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system#Market_share "Mobile operating system")

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Android_phone.jpg/250px-Android_phone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Android_phone.jpg)

[Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") is the most popular [mobile operating system](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system"), and is used by virtually all mobile phones, except for [iPhone](/wiki/IPhone "IPhone") models, which use [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS").

By Q1 2018, [mobile operating systems](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system") on [smartphones](/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone") included [Google](/wiki/Google "Google")'s dominant [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") (and variants) and [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS") which combined had an almost 100% market share.[[191]](#cite_note-194)

title: Usage share of operating systems

By Q1 2018, [mobile operating systems](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system") on [smartphones](/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone") included [Google](/wiki/Google "Google")'s dominant [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") (and variants) and [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS") which combined had an almost 100% market share.[[191]](#cite_note-194)

Smartphone penetration vs. desktop use differs substantially by country. Some countries, like Russia, still have smartphone use as low as 22.35% (as a fraction of all web use),[[192]](#cite_note-195) but in most western countries, smartphone use is close to 50% of all web use.[[193]](#cite_note-196) This doesn't mean that only half of the population has a smartphone, could mean almost all have, just that other platforms have about equal use. Smartphone usage share in developing countries is much higher – in Bangladesh, for example, Android smartphones had up to 84% and currently 70% share,[[109]](#cite_note-Bangladesh-110) and in Mali smartphones had over 90% (up to 95%) share for almost two years.[[194]](#cite_note-197)[[195]](#cite_note-198) (A section below has more information on regional trends on the move to smartphones.)

There is a clear correlation between the GDP per capita of a country and that country's respective smartphone OS market share, with users in the richest countries being much more likely to choose Apple's iPhone, with Google's Android being predominant elsewhere.[[196]](#cite_note-199)[[197]](#cite_note-200)[[198]](#cite_note-auto2-201)

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
### Tablet computers OS by usage

[Tablet computers](/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer"), or simply *tablets*, became a significant OS market share category starting with Apple's [iPad](/wiki/IPad "IPad"). In Q1 2018, iOS had 65.03% market share and Android had 34.58% market share.[[209]](#cite_note-auto3-214) Windows tablets may not get classified as such by some analysts, and thus barely register; e.g. [2-in-1 PCs](/wiki/2-in-1_PC "2-in-1 PC") may get classified as "desktops", not tablets.

Since 2016, in South America (and Cuba[[210]](#cite_note-215) in North America), Android tablets have gained majority,[[211]](#cite_note-216) and in Asia in 2017 Android was slightly more popular than the iPad, which was at 49.05% usage share in October 2015.[[212]](#cite_note-217)[[213]](#cite_note-218)[[214]](#cite_note-219) In Africa, Android tablets are much more popular while elsewhere the iPad has a safe margin.

As of March 2015[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Usage_share_of_operating_systems&action=edit), Android has made steady gains to becoming the most popular tablet operating system:[[215]](#cite_note-220) that is the trend in many countries, having already gained the majority in large countries (India at 63.25%,[[216]](#cite_note-221) and in Indonesia at 62.22%[[217]](#cite_note-222)) and in the African continent with Android at 62.22% (first to gain Android majority in late 2014),[[218]](#cite_note-223) with steady gains from 20.98% in August 2012[[219]](#cite_note-224) (Egypt at 62.37%,[[220]](#cite_note-gs.statcounter.com-225) Zimbabwe at 62.04%[[220]](#cite_note-gs.statcounter.com-225)), and South America at 51.09% in July 2015.[[221]](#cite_note-226) (Peru at 52.96%[[222]](#cite_note-227)). Asia is at 46%.[[223]](#cite_note-228) In Nepal, Android gained majority lead in November 2014 but lost it down to 41.35% with iOS at 56.51%.[[224]](#cite_note-229) In Taiwan, as of October 2016, Android after having gained a confident majority, has been on a losing streak.[[225]](#cite_note-230) China is a major exception to Android gaining market share in Asia (there Android [phablets](/wiki/Phablet "Phablet") are much more popular than Android tablets, while similar devices get classified as smartphones) where the iPad/iOS is at 82.84% in March 2015.[[226]](#cite_note-231)

See also: [Usage share of web browsers § Crossover to smartphones having majority share](/wiki/Usage_share_of_web_browsers#Crossover_to_smartphones_having_majority_share "Usage share of web browsers")

According to [StatCounter](/wiki/StatCounter "StatCounter") web use statistics (a proxy for all use), smartphones are more popular than desktop computers globally (and Android in particular more popular than Windows). Including tablets with mobiles/smartphones, as they also run so-called [mobile operating systems](/wiki/Mobile_operating_systems "Mobile operating systems"), even in the United States (and most countries) are mobiles including tablets more popular than other (older originally made for desktops) operating systems (such as Windows and macOS). Windows in the US (at 33.42%) has only 8% head-start (2.55-percentage points) over iOS only; with Android, that mobile operating system and iOS have 52.14% majority.[[236]](#cite_note-241) Alternatively, Apple, with iOS plus their non-mobile macOS (9.33%) has 20% more share (6.7-percentage points more) than Microsoft's Windows in the country where both companies were built.

Although desktop computers are still popular in many countries (while overall down to 44.9% in the first quarter of 2017[[237]](#cite_note-Q1_2017-242)), smartphones are more popular even in many developed countries. In Ireland, smartphone use at 45.55% outnumbers desktop use and mobile as a whole gains majority when including the tablet share at 9.12%.[[239]](#cite_note-244)[[240]](#cite_note-245) Spain was also slightly desktop-minority. As of July 2019, Sweden had been desktop-minority for eight weeks in a row.[[241]](#cite_note-246)

In the week of 7–13 November 2016, smartphones alone (without tablets) overtook desktop for the first time, albeit for a short period.[[245]](#cite_note-250) Examples of mobile-majority countries include Paraguay in South America, Poland in Europe and Turkey and most of Asia and Africa. Some of the world is still desktop-majority, with for example the United States at 54.89% (but not on all days).[[246]](#cite_note-251) However, in some [territories of the United States](/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"), such as [Puerto Rico](/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"),[[247]](#cite_note-252) desktop is significantly under majority, with Windows just under 25%, overtaken by Android.

Two continents have already crossed over to mobile-majority (because of Android), based on StatCounters web use statistics. In June 2015, [Asia](/wiki/Asia "Asia") became the first continent where mobile overtook desktop[[292]](#cite_note-297) (followed by [Africa](/wiki/Africa "Africa") in August;[[293]](#cite_note-298) while [Nigeria](/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") had mobile majority in October 2011,[[294]](#cite_note-299)[[295]](#cite_note-300) because of [Symbian](/wiki/Symbian "Symbian") – that later had 51% share, then [Series 40](/wiki/Series_40 "Series 40") dominating, followed by Android as dominating operating system[[296]](#cite_note-301)) and as far back as October 2014, they had reported this trend on a large scale in a press release: "Mobile usage has already overtaken desktop in several countries including [India](/wiki/India "India"), [South Africa](/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") and [Saudi Arabia](/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia")".[[297]](#cite_note-302) In India, desktop went from majority, in July 2012, down to 32%.[[298]](#cite_note-303) In Bangladesh desktop went from majority, in May 2013, down to 17%, with Android alone now accounting for majority web use.[[299]](#cite_note-304) Only a few African countries were still desktop-majority[[300]](#cite_note-305) and many have a large mobile majority including [Ethiopia](/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia") and [Kenya](/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), where mobile usage is over 72%.[[301]](#cite_note-306)

text:
While some analysts count tablets with desktops (as some of them run Windows), others count them with mobile phones (as the vast majority of tablets run so-called [mobile operating systems](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system"), such as [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") or [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS") on the [iPad](/wiki/IPad "IPad")). iPad has a clear lead globally, but has clearly lost the majority to Android in South America,[[306]](#cite_note-311) and a number of Eastern European countries such as Poland; lost virtually all African countries and has lost the majority twice in Asia, but gained the majority back (while many individual countries, e.g. India and most of the middle East have clear Android majority on tablets).[[307]](#cite_note-312) Android on tablets is thus second most popular after the iPad.[[308]](#cite_note-313)

In March 2015, for the first time in the US, the number of mobile-only adult internet users exceeded the number of desktop-only internet users with 11.6% of the digital population only using mobile compared to 10.6% only using desktop; this also means the majority, 78%, use both desktop and mobile to access the internet.[[309]](#cite_note-desktop-to-mobile-314) A few smaller countries in North America, such as Haiti (because of Android) have gone mobile majority (mobile went to up to 72.35%, and is at 64.43% in February 2016).[[310]](#cite_note-315)

## Public servers on the Internet

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Rack001.jpg/250px-Rack001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Rack001.jpg)

[Servers](/wiki/Server_(computing) "Server (computing)") in a [colocation centre](/wiki/Colocation_centre "Colocation centre")

[Internet based servers](/wiki/Server_(computing) "Server (computing)")' [market share](/wiki/Market_share "Market share") can be measured with statistical surveys of publicly accessible servers, such as [web servers](/wiki/Web_server "Web server"), [mail servers](/wiki/Mail_server "Mail server")[[314]](#cite_note-319) or [DNS servers](/wiki/DNS_server "DNS server") on the Internet: the operating systems powering such servers are found by inspecting raw response messages. This method gives insight only into market share of operating systems that are publicly accessible on the Internet.

There will be differences in the result depending on how the sample is done and observations weighted. Usually the surveys are not based on a random sample of all IP addresses, domain names, hosts or organisations, but on servers found by some other method.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Additionally, many domains and IP addresses may be served by one host and some domains may be served by several hosts or by one host with several IP addresses.

## Mainframes

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/IBM_System_z10.jpg/250px-IBM_System_z10.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:IBM_System_z10.jpg)

IBM's [System z10](/wiki/IBM_System_z10 "IBM System z10")

[Mainframes](/wiki/Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") are larger and more powerful than most servers, but not [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer"). They are used to process large sets of data, for example [enterprise resource planning](/wiki/Enterprise_resource_planning "Enterprise resource planning") or [credit card transactions](/wiki/Transaction_processing "Transaction processing").

The most common operating system for mainframes is IBM's proprietary [z/OS](/wiki/Z/OS "Z/OS").[[322]](#cite_note-327)[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Operating systems for [IBM Z](/wiki/IBM_Z "IBM Z") generation hardware include z/OS,[[323]](#cite_note-IBM-Anti-Trust-328) [Linux on IBM Z](/wiki/Linux_on_IBM_Z "Linux on IBM Z"), [z/TPF](/wiki/Transaction_Processing_Facility "Transaction Processing Facility"), [VSE](/wiki/VSE_(operating_system) "VSE (operating system)") and [z/VM](/wiki/Z/VM "Z/VM").

[Gartner](/wiki/Gartner "Gartner") reported on 23 December 2008 that Linux on System z was used on approximately 28% of the "customer z base" and that they expected this to increase to over 50% in the following five years.[[324]](#cite_note-gartnovell-329) Of Linux on IBM Z, [Red Hat](/wiki/Red_Hat "Red Hat") and [Micro Focus](/wiki/Micro_Focus "Micro Focus") compete to sell [RHEL](/wiki/Red_Hat_Enterprise_Linux "Red Hat Enterprise Linux") and [SLES](/wiki/SUSE_Linux_Enterprise_Server "SUSE Linux Enterprise Server") respectively:

title: Usage share of operating systems
text:
### Decline

Like today's trend of mobile devices from personal computers,[[309]](#cite_note-desktop-to-mobile-314) in 1984, for the first time, estimated sales of desktop computers ($11.6 billion) exceeded mainframe computers ($11.4 billion). IBM received the vast majority of mainframe revenue.[[326]](#cite_note-sanger19840205-331)

During the 1990s, companies found that servers based on [microcomputer](/wiki/Microcomputer "Microcomputer") designs could be deployed at a fraction of the acquisition price and offer local users much greater control over their own systems given the IT policies and practices at that time. Terminals used for interacting with mainframe systems were gradually replaced by personal computers. Consequently, demand plummeted and new mainframe installations were restricted mainly to financial services and government. In the early 1990s, there was a rough consensus among industry analysts that the mainframe was a dying market as mainframe platforms were increasingly replaced by personal computer networks.[[327]](#cite_note-332)

During the 1990s, companies found that servers based on [microcomputer](/wiki/Microcomputer "Microcomputer") designs could be deployed at a fraction of the acquisition price and offer local users much greater control over their own systems given the IT policies and practices at that time. Terminals used for interacting with mainframe systems were gradually replaced by personal computers. Consequently, demand plummeted and new mainframe installations were restricted mainly to financial services and government. In the early 1990s, there was a rough consensus among industry analysts that the mainframe was a dying market as mainframe platforms were increasingly replaced by personal computer networks.[[327]](#cite_note-332)

In 2012, [NASA](/wiki/NASA "NASA") powered down its last mainframe, an [IBM System z9](/wiki/IBM_System_z9 "IBM System z9").[[328]](#cite_note-333) However, IBM's successor to the z9, the [z10](/wiki/IBM_System_z10 "IBM System z10"), led a New York Times reporter to state four years earlier that "mainframe technology—hardware, software and services—remains a large and lucrative business for IBM, and mainframes are still the back-office engines behind the world's financial markets and much of global commerce".[[329]](#cite_note-334) As of 2010[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Usage_share_of_operating_systems&action=edit), while mainframe technology represented less than 3% of IBM's revenues, it "continue[d] to play an outsized role in Big Blue's results".[[330]](#cite_note-335)

## Supercomputers

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Sierra_Supercomputer_%2848002385338%29.jpg/250px-Sierra_Supercomputer_%2848002385338%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Sierra_Supercomputer_(48002385338).jpg)

[Sierra](/wiki/Sierra_(supercomputer) "Sierra (supercomputer)") is primarily used for the [stockpile stewardship](/wiki/Stockpile_stewardship "Stockpile stewardship") program of the United States.

The [TOP500](/wiki/TOP500 "TOP500") project lists and ranks the 500 fastest [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer") for which benchmark results are submitted. Since the early 1990s, the field of supercomputers has been dominated by [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") or [Unix-like](/wiki/Unix-like "Unix-like") operating systems, and starting in 2017, every top 500 fastest supercomputer uses [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") as its [supercomputer operating system](/wiki/Supercomputer_operating_systems "Supercomputer operating systems").

The last supercomputer to rank #1 while using an operating system other than Linux was [ASCI White](/wiki/ASCI_White "ASCI White"), which ran [AIX](/wiki/AIX "AIX"). It held the title from November 2000 to November 2001,[[331]](#cite_note-336) and was decommissioned in 2006. Then in June 2017, two AIX computers held rank 493 and 494,[[332]](#cite_note-TechFAE201706-337) the last non-Linux systems before they dropped off the list.

An **operating system** (**OS**) is [system software](/wiki/System_software "System software") that manages [computer hardware](/wiki/Computer_hardware "Computer hardware") and [software](/wiki/Software "Software") resources, and provides common [services](/wiki/Daemon_(computing) "Daemon (computing)") for [computer programs](/wiki/Computer_program "Computer program").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

[Time-sharing](/wiki/Time-sharing "Time-sharing") operating systems [schedule tasks](/wiki/Scheduler_(computing) "Scheduler (computing)") for efficient use of the system and may also include accounting software for cost allocation of [processor time](/wiki/Scheduling_(computing) "Scheduling (computing)"), [mass storage](/wiki/Mass_storage "Mass storage"), peripherals, and other resources.

title: Operating system
text:
[Time-sharing](/wiki/Time-sharing "Time-sharing") operating systems [schedule tasks](/wiki/Scheduler_(computing) "Scheduler (computing)") for efficient use of the system and may also include accounting software for cost allocation of [processor time](/wiki/Scheduling_(computing) "Scheduling (computing)"), [mass storage](/wiki/Mass_storage "Mass storage"), peripherals, and other resources.

For hardware functions such as [input and output](/wiki/Input_and_output "Input and output") and [memory allocation](/wiki/Memory_allocation "Memory allocation"), the operating system acts as an intermediary between programs and the computer hardware,[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) although the application code is usually executed directly by the hardware and frequently makes [system calls](/wiki/System_call "System call") to an OS function or is [interrupted](/wiki/Interrupt "Interrupt") by it. Operating systems are found on many devices that contain a computer – from cellular phones and video game consoles to [web servers](/wiki/Web_server "Web server") and [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer").

title: Operating system
text:
For hardware functions such as [input and output](/wiki/Input_and_output "Input and output") and [memory allocation](/wiki/Memory_allocation "Memory allocation"), the operating system acts as an intermediary between programs and the computer hardware,[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) although the application code is usually executed directly by the hardware and frequently makes [system calls](/wiki/System_call "System call") to an OS function or is [interrupted](/wiki/Interrupt "Interrupt") by it. Operating systems are found on many devices that contain a computer – from cellular phones and video game consoles to [web servers](/wiki/Web_server "Web server") and [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer").

As of November 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Operating_system&action=edit), [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") is the most popular operating system, with a 38% market share, followed by [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") at 33%, [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS") and [iPadOS](/wiki/IPadOS "IPadOS") at 15%, [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") at 4%, and [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") at 1%. Android, iOS, and iPadOS are operating systems for mobile devices such as smartphones, while Windows, macOS, and Linux are for desktop computers.[[4]](#cite_note-gs.statcounter.com-4) [Linux distributions](/wiki/Linux_distribution "Linux distribution") are dominant in the server and supercomputing sectors and number in the thousands.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) Other specialized classes of operating systems (special-purpose operating systems),[[7]](#cite_note-auto-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) such as [embedded](/wiki/Embedded_system "Embedded system") and real-time systems, exist for many applications. [Security-focused operating systems](/wiki/Security-focused_operating_system "Security-focused operating system") also exist. Some operating systems have low system requirements (e.g. [light-weight Linux distribution](/wiki/Light-weight_Linux_distribution "Light-weight Linux distribution")). Others may have higher system requirements.

title: Operating system
text:
## Definition and purpose

An operating system is difficult to define,[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20234-9) but has been called "the [layer of software](/wiki/Abstraction_layer "Abstraction layer") that manages a computer's resources for its users and their [applications](/wiki/Application_software "Application software")".[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20146-10) Operating systems include the software that is always running, called a [kernel](/wiki/Kernel_(operating_system) "Kernel (operating system)")—but can include other software as well.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20234-9)[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilberschatz_et_al.20186-11) The two other types of programs that can run on a computer are [system programs](/wiki/System_software "System software")—which are associated with the operating system, but may not be part of the kernel—and applications—all other software.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilberschatz_et_al.20186-11)

There are three main purposes that an operating system fulfills:[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20147-12)

title: Operating system
text:
An operating system is difficult to define,[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20234-9) but has been called "the [layer of software](/wiki/Abstraction_layer "Abstraction layer") that manages a computer's resources for its users and their [applications](/wiki/Application_software "Application software")".[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20146-10) Operating systems include the software that is always running, called a [kernel](/wiki/Kernel_(operating_system) "Kernel (operating system)")—but can include other software as well.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20234-9)[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilberschatz_et_al.20186-11) The two other types of programs that can run on a computer are [system programs](/wiki/System_software "System software")—which are associated with the operating system, but may not be part of the kernel—and applications—all other software.[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilberschatz_et_al.20186-11)

There are three main purposes that an operating system fulfills:[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20147-12)

- Operating systems allocate resources between different applications, deciding when they will receive [central processing unit](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPU) time or space in [memory](/wiki/Computer_memory "Computer memory").[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20147-12) On modern [personal computers](/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer"), users often want to run several applications at once. In order to ensure that one program cannot monopolize the computer's limited hardware resources, the operating system gives each application a share of the resource, either in time (CPU) or space (memory).[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20149–10-13)[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20236–7-14) The operating system also must isolate applications from each other to protect them from errors and security vulnerabilities in another application's code, but enable communications between different applications.[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201410-15)
- Operating systems provide an interface that abstracts the details of [hardware](/wiki/Computer_hardware "Computer hardware") access (such as physical memory) to make things easier for programmers.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20147-12)[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20235-16) [Virtualization](/wiki/Virtualization "Virtualization") also enables the operating system to mask limited hardware resources; for example, [virtual memory](/wiki/Virtual_memory "Virtual memory") can provide a program with the illusion of nearly unlimited memory that exceeds the computer's actual memory.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201411-17)

title: Operating system
text: - Operating systems provide common services, such as an interface for accessing network and disk devices. This enables an application to be run on different hardware without needing to be rewritten.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin20147,_9,_13-18) Which services to include in an operating system varies greatly, and this functionality makes up the great majority of code for most operating systems.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201412–13-19)

title: Operating system
text: ## Types of operating systems
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Multicomputer operating systems

With [multiprocessors](/wiki/Multiprocessor "Multiprocessor") multiple CPUs share memory. A [multicomputer](/wiki/Multicomputer "Multicomputer") or [cluster computer](/wiki/Cluster_computer "Cluster computer") has multiple CPUs, each of which [has its own memory](/wiki/Distributed_memory "Distributed memory").
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
With [multiprocessors](/wiki/Multiprocessor "Multiprocessor") multiple CPUs share memory. A [multicomputer](/wiki/Multicomputer "Multicomputer") or [cluster computer](/wiki/Cluster_computer "Cluster computer") has multiple CPUs, each of which [has its own memory](/wiki/Distributed_memory "Distributed memory").

Multicomputers were developed because large multiprocessors are difficult to engineer and prohibitively expensive;[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023557-20) they are universal in [cloud computing](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") because of the size of the machine needed.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023558-21) The different CPUs often need to send and receive messages to each other;[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023565-22) to ensure good performance, the operating systems for these machines need to minimize this copying of [packets](/wiki/Network_packet "Network packet").[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023562-23) Newer systems are often [multiqueue](/w/index.php?title=Multiqueue&action=edit&redlink=1 "Multiqueue (page does not exist)")—separating groups of users into separate [queues](/wiki/Priority_queue "Priority queue")—to reduce the need for packet copying and support more concurrent users.[[24]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023563-24) Another technique is [remote direct memory access](/wiki/Remote_direct_memory_access "Remote direct memory access"), which enables each CPU to access memory belonging to other CPUs.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023565-22) Multicomputer operating systems often support [remote procedure calls](/wiki/Remote_procedure_call "Remote procedure call") where a CPU can call a [procedure](/wiki/Procedural_programming "Procedural programming") on another CPU,[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023569-25) or [distributed shared memory](/wiki/Distributed_shared_memory "Distributed shared memory"), in which the operating system uses [virtualization](/wiki/Virtualization "Virtualization") to generate shared memory that does not physically exist.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023571-26)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Distributed systems

A [distributed system](/wiki/Distributed_system "Distributed system") is a group of distinct, [networked](/wiki/Computer_network "Computer network") computers—each of which might have their own operating system and file system. Unlike multicomputers, they may be dispersed anywhere in the world.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023579-27) [Middleware](/wiki/Middleware "Middleware"), an additional software layer between the operating system and applications, is often used to improve consistency. Although it functions similarly to an operating system, it is not a true operating system.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos2023581-28)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Embedded

[Embedded operating systems](/wiki/Embedded_operating_system "Embedded operating system") are designed to be used in [embedded computer systems](/wiki/Embedded_system "Embedded system"), whether they are [internet of things](/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things") objects or not connected to a network. Embedded systems include many household appliances. The distinguishing factor is that they do not load user-installed software. Consequently, they do not need protection between different applications, enabling simpler designs. Very small operating systems might run in less than 10 [kilobytes](/wiki/Kilobytes "Kilobytes"),[[29]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202337–38-29) and the smallest are for [smart cards](/wiki/Smart_cards "Smart cards").[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202339-30) Examples include [Embedded Linux](/wiki/Embedded_Linux "Embedded Linux"), [QNX](/wiki/QNX "QNX"), [VxWorks](/wiki/VxWorks "VxWorks"), and the extra-small systems [RIOT](/wiki/RIOT_(operating_system) "RIOT (operating system)") and [TinyOS](/wiki/TinyOS "TinyOS").[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202338-31)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Real-time

A [real-time operating system](/wiki/Real-time_operating_system "Real-time operating system") is an operating system that guarantees to process [events](/wiki/Event_(computing) "Event (computing)") or data by or at a specific moment in time. Hard real-time systems require exact timing and are common in [manufacturing](/wiki/Manufacturing "Manufacturing"), [avionics](/wiki/Avionics "Avionics"), military, and other similar uses.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202338-31) With soft real-time systems, the occasional missed event is acceptable; this category often includes audio or multimedia systems, as well as smartphones.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202338-31) In order for hard real-time systems be sufficiently exact in their timing, often they are just a library with no protection between applications, such as [eCos](/wiki/ECos "ECos").[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202338-31)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Hypervisor

A [hypervisor](/wiki/Hypervisor "Hypervisor") is an operating system that runs a [virtual machine](/wiki/Virtual_machine "Virtual machine"). The virtual machine is an application that emulates hardware; in other words, it operates as much as possible like the actual hardware the operating system was designed to run on.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201411-17)[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilberschatz_et_al.2018701-32) Virtual machines can be paused, saved, and resumed, making them useful for operating systems research, development,[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESilberschatz_et_al.2018705-33) and debugging.[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201412-34) They also enhance portability by enabling applications to be run on a computer even if they are not compatible with the base operating system.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201411-17)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Library

A *library operating system* (libOS) is one in which the services that a typical operating system provides, such as networking, are provided in the form of [libraries](/wiki/Library_(computing) "Library (computing)") and composed with a single application and configuration code to construct a [unikernel](/wiki/Unikernel "Unikernel"):
[[35]](#cite_note-Unikernels-35) a specialized (only the absolute necessary pieces of code are extracted from libraries and bound together
[[36]](#cite_note-Unikraft-Build-Process-36)), [single address space](/wiki/Single_address_space_operating_system "Single address space operating system"), machine image that can be deployed to cloud or embedded environments.

The operating system code and application code are not executed in separated [protection domains](/wiki/Protection_ring "Protection ring") (there is only a single application running, at least conceptually, so there is no need to prevent interference between applications) and OS services are accessed via simple library calls (potentially [inlining](/wiki/Inline_expansion "Inline expansion") them based on compiler thresholds), without the usual overhead of [context switches](/wiki/Context_switch "Context switch"),
[[37]](#cite_note-rise-of-libOS-37) in a way similarly to embedded and real-time OSes. This overhead is not negligible: to the direct cost of mode switching it's necessary to add the indirect pollution of important processor structures (like [CPU caches](/wiki/CPU_cache "CPU cache"), the [instruction pipeline](/wiki/Instruction_pipelining "Instruction pipelining"), and so on) which affects both user-mode and kernel-mode performance.
[[38]](#cite_note-FlexSC-38)

## History

Main article: [History of operating systems](/wiki/History_of_operating_systems "History of operating systems")

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/IBM_system_360-50_console_-_MfK_Bern.jpg/250px-IBM_system_360-50_console_-_MfK_Bern.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:IBM_system_360-50_console_-_MfK_Bern.jpg)

title: Operating system
text:
IBM System/360 Model 50 operator's console and CPU; the operator's console is a [terminal](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal") used by the operating system to communicate with the operator.

The first computers in the late 1940s and 1950s were directly programmed either with [plugboards](/wiki/Plugboard "Plugboard") or with [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code") inputted on media such as [punch cards](/wiki/Punch_card "Punch card"), without [programming languages](/wiki/Programming_language "Programming language") or operating systems.[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20238-39) After the introduction of the [transistor](/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") in the mid-1950s, [mainframes](/wiki/Mainframe "Mainframe") began to be built. These still needed professional operators[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20238-39) who manually do what a modern operating system would do, such as scheduling programs to run,[[40]](#cite_note-OSTEP_book-40) but mainframes still had rudimentary operating systems such as [Fortran Monitor System](/wiki/Fortran_Monitor_System "Fortran Monitor System") (FMS) and [IBSYS](/wiki/IBSYS "IBSYS").[[41]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202310-41) In the 1960s, [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM") introduced the first series of intercompatible computers ([System/360](/wiki/System/360 "System/360")). All of them ran the same operating system—[OS/360](/wiki/OS/360 "OS/360")—which consisted of millions of lines of [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language") that had thousands of [bugs](/wiki/Software_bug "Software bug"). The OS/360 also was the first popular operating system to support [multiprogramming](/wiki/Multiprogramming "Multiprogramming"), such that, if one job is blocked waiting for an [input/output](/wiki/Input/output "Input/output") (I/O) operation to complete, another job can use the CPU.

Holding multiple jobs in [memory](/wiki/Memory_(computing) "Memory (computing)") required memory partitioning and safeguards against one job accessing the memory allocated to a different job.[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202311–12-42)

title: Operating system
text:
Holding multiple jobs in [memory](/wiki/Memory_(computing) "Memory (computing)") required memory partitioning and safeguards against one job accessing the memory allocated to a different job.[[42]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202311–12-42)

Around the same time, [teleprinters](/wiki/Teleprinter "Teleprinter") began to be used as [terminals](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal") so multiple users could access the computer simultaneously. The operating system [MULTICS](/wiki/MULTICS "MULTICS") was intended to allow hundreds of users to access a large computer. Despite its limited adoption, it can be considered the precursor to [cloud computing](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing"). The [UNIX](/wiki/UNIX "UNIX") operating system originated as a development of MULTICS for a single user.[[43]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202313–14-43) Because UNIX's [source code](/wiki/Source_code "Source code") was available, it became the basis of other, incompatible operating systems, of which the most successful were [AT&T](/wiki/AT%26T "AT&T")'s [System V](/wiki/System_V "System V") and the [University of California](/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley")'s [Berkeley Software Distribution](/wiki/Berkeley_Software_Distribution "Berkeley Software Distribution") (BSD).[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202314–15-44) To increase compatibility, the [IEEE](/wiki/IEEE "IEEE") released the [POSIX](/wiki/POSIX "POSIX") standard for operating system [application programming interfaces](/wiki/Application_programming_interface "Application programming interface") (APIs), which is supported by most UNIX systems. [MINIX](/wiki/MINIX "MINIX") was a stripped-down version of UNIX, developed in 1987 for educational uses, that inspired the commercially available, [free software](/wiki/Free_software "Free software") [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux").

### Microcomputers

[Command-line interface](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface") of the [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") operating system

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/95/System_1_File_Edit.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](/wiki/File:System_1_File_Edit.png)

[Graphical user interface](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") of a [Macintosh](/wiki/Macintosh "Macintosh")

The invention of [large scale integration](/wiki/Large_scale_integration "Large scale integration") enabled the production of [personal computers](/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") (initially called [microcomputers](/wiki/Microcomputer "Microcomputer")) from around 1980.[[46]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202315–16-46) For around five years, the [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") (Control Program for Microcomputers) was the most popular operating system for microcomputers.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202316-47) Later, IBM bought a [disk operating system](/wiki/Disk_operating_system "Disk operating system") from [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"), which IBM sold as [IBM PC DOS](/wiki/IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS") and Microsoft branded as [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") (MicroSoft Disk Operating System) and was widely used on [IBM PC compatible](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") microcomputers. Later versions increased their sophistication, in part by borrowing features from UNIX.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202316-47)

Later versions increased their sophistication, in part by borrowing features from UNIX.[[47]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202316-47)

The first popular computer to use a [graphical user interface](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") (GUI) was [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s [Macintosh](/wiki/Macintosh "Macintosh"). The GUI proved much more [user friendly](/wiki/User_friendly "User friendly") than the text-only [command-line interface](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface") of earlier operating systems. This success prompted Microsoft to add a GUI overlay to MS-DOS called [Windows](/wiki/Windows "Windows"). Windows later was rewritten as a stand-alone operating system, [Windows NT](/wiki/Windows_NT "Windows NT"), borrowing so many features from another OS ([VAX/VMS](/wiki/VAX/VMS "VAX/VMS")) that a large [legal settlement](/wiki/Legal_settlement "Legal settlement") was paid.[[48]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202317-48) In the 21st century, Windows continues to be popular on personal computers but has less [market share](/wiki/Market_share "Market share") of servers. UNIX operating systems, especially Linux, are the most popular on [enterprise systems](/wiki/Enterprise_system "Enterprise system") and servers but are also used on [mobile devices](/wiki/Mobile_device "Mobile device") and many other computer systems.[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos202318-49)

title: Operating system
text:
## Components

The components of an operating system are designed to ensure that various parts of a computer function cohesively. With the de facto obsoletion of [DOS](/wiki/Disk_Operating_System "Disk Operating System"), all user [software](/wiki/Software "Software") must interact with the operating system to access hardware.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
### Kernel

Main article: [Kernel (operating system)](/wiki/Kernel_(operating_system) "Kernel (operating system)")

The kernel is the part of the operating system that provides [protection](/wiki/Protection_ring "Protection ring") between different applications and users. This protection is key to improving reliability by keeping errors isolated to one program, as well as security by limiting the power of [malicious software](/wiki/Malicious_software "Malicious software") and protecting private data, and ensuring that one program cannot monopolize the computer's resources.[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201439–40-51) Most operating systems have two modes of operation:[[52]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETanenbaumBos20232-52) in [user mode](/wiki/User_mode "User mode"), the hardware checks that the software is only executing legal instructions, whereas the kernel has [unrestricted powers](/wiki/Privilege_(computing) "Privilege (computing)") and is not subject to these checks.[[53]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201441,_45-53) The kernel also manages [memory](/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") for other processes and controls access to [input/output](/wiki/Input/output "Input/output") devices.[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndersonDahlin201452–53-54)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
#### Program execution

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Kernel_Layout.svg/250px-Kernel_Layout.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Kernel_Layout.svg)

A kernel connects the application software to the hardware of a computer.

The operating system provides an interface between an application program and the computer hardware, so that an application program can interact with the hardware only by obeying rules and procedures programmed into the operating system. The operating system is also a set of services which simplify development and execution of application programs. Executing an application program typically involves the creation of a [process](/wiki/Process_(computing) "Process (computing)") by the operating system [kernel](/wiki/Kernel_(operating_system) "Kernel (operating system)"), which assigns memory space and other resources, establishes a priority for the process in multi-tasking systems, loads program binary code into memory, and initiates execution of the application program, which then interacts with the user and with hardware devices. However, in some systems an application can request that the operating system execute another application within the same process, either as a subroutine or in a separate thread, e.g., the **LINK** and **ATTACH** facilities of [OS/360 and successors](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors").
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
#### Interrupts

Main article: [Interrupt](/wiki/Interrupt "Interrupt")

An [interrupt](/wiki/Interrupt "Interrupt") (also known as an [abort](/wiki/Abort_(computing) "Abort (computing)"), [exception](/wiki/Exception_handling "Exception handling"), *fault*, [signal](/wiki/Signal_(IPC) "Signal (IPC)"),[[55]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388_quote1-55) or *trap*)[[56]](#cite_note-Hyde_1996-56) provides an efficient way for most operating systems to react to the environment. Interrupts cause the [central processing unit](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPU) to have a [control flow](/wiki/Control_flow "Control flow") change away from the currently running program to an [interrupt handler](/wiki/Interrupt_handler "Interrupt handler"), also known as an interrupt service routine (ISR).[[57]](#cite_note-sco-ch5-p308_a-57)[[58]](#cite_note-osc-ch2-p32_a-58) An interrupt service routine may cause the [central processing unit](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPU) to have a [context switch](/wiki/Context_switch "Context switch").[[59]](#cite_note-osc-ch4-p105-59)[[a]](#cite_note-60) The details of how a computer processes an interrupt vary from architecture to architecture, and the details of how interrupt service routines behave vary from operating system to operating system.[[60]](#cite_note-osc-ch2-p31-61) However, several interrupt functions are common.[[60]](#cite_note-osc-ch2-p31-61) The architecture and operating system must:[[60]](#cite_note-osc-ch2-p31-61)

1. transfer control to an interrupt service routine.
2. save the state of the currently running process.
3. restore the state after the interrupt is serviced.

title: Operating system
text:
##### Software interrupt

A software interrupt is a message to a [process](/wiki/Process_(computing) "Process (computing)") that an event has occurred.[[55]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388_quote1-55) This contrasts with a *hardware interrupt*—which is a message to the [central processing unit](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPU) that an event has occurred.[[61]](#cite_note-osc-ch2-p30-62) Software interrupts are similar to hardware interrupts—there is a change away from the currently running process.[[62]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388_quote2-63) Similarly, both hardware and software interrupts execute an [interrupt service routine](/wiki/Interrupt_handler "Interrupt handler").

Software interrupts may be normally occurring events. It is expected that a [time slice](/wiki/Preemption_(computing)#Time_slice "Preemption (computing)") will occur, so the kernel will have to perform a [context switch](/wiki/Context_switch "Context switch").[[63]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388_quote3-64) A [computer program](/wiki/Computer_program "Computer program") may set a timer to go off after a few seconds in case too much data causes an algorithm to take too long.[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65)

Software interrupts may be error conditions, such as a malformed [machine instruction](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code").[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65) However, the most common error conditions are [division by zero](/wiki/Division_by_zero "Division by zero") and [accessing an invalid memory address](/wiki/Segmentation_fault "Segmentation fault").[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Operating system

title: Operating system
text:
Software interrupts may be error conditions, such as a malformed [machine instruction](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code").[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65) However, the most common error conditions are [division by zero](/wiki/Division_by_zero "Division by zero") and [accessing an invalid memory address](/wiki/Segmentation_fault "Segmentation fault").[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65)

[Users](/wiki/User_(computing) "User (computing)") can send messages to the kernel to modify the behavior of a currently running process.[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65) For example, in the [command-line environment](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface"), pressing the *interrupt character* (usually [Control-C](/wiki/Control-C "Control-C")) might terminate the currently running process.[[64]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p388-65)

To generate *software interrupts* for [x86](/wiki/X86 "X86") CPUs, the [INT](/wiki/INT_(x86_instruction) "INT (x86 instruction)") [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language") instruction is available.[[65]](#cite_note-intel-developer-66) The syntax is `INT X`, where `X` is the offset number (in [hexadecimal](/wiki/Hexadecimal "Hexadecimal") format) to the [interrupt vector table](/wiki/Interrupt_vector_table "Interrupt vector table").

title: Operating system
text:
##### Signal

To generate *software interrupts* in [Unix-like](/wiki/Unix-like "Unix-like") operating systems, the `kill(pid,signum)` [system call](/wiki/System_call "System call") will send a [signal](/wiki/Signal_(IPC) "Signal (IPC)") to another process.[[66]](#cite_note-duos-p200-67) `pid` is the [process identifier](/wiki/Process_identifier "Process identifier") of the receiving process. `signum` is the signal number (in [mnemonic](/wiki/Mnemonic "Mnemonic") format)[[b]](#cite_note-68) to be sent. (The abrasive name of `kill` was chosen because early implementations only terminated the process.)[[67]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p400-69)

title: Operating system
text:
To generate *software interrupts* in [Unix-like](/wiki/Unix-like "Unix-like") operating systems, the `kill(pid,signum)` [system call](/wiki/System_call "System call") will send a [signal](/wiki/Signal_(IPC) "Signal (IPC)") to another process.[[66]](#cite_note-duos-p200-67) `pid` is the [process identifier](/wiki/Process_identifier "Process identifier") of the receiving process. `signum` is the signal number (in [mnemonic](/wiki/Mnemonic "Mnemonic") format)[[b]](#cite_note-68) to be sent. (The abrasive name of `kill` was chosen because early implementations only terminated the process.)[[67]](#cite_note-lpi-ch20-p400-69)

In Unix-like operating systems, *signals* inform processes of the occurrence of asynchronous events.[[66]](#cite_note-duos-p200-67) To communicate asynchronously, interrupts are required.[[68]](#cite_note-sco-ch5-p308_b-70) One reason a process needs to asynchronously communicate to another process is to solve a variation of the classic [reader/writer problem](/wiki/Readers%E2%80%93writers_problem "Readers–writers problem").[[69]](#cite_note-osc-p182-71) The writer receives a pipe from the [shell](/wiki/Shell_(computing) "Shell (computing)") for its output to be sent to the reader's input stream.[[70]](#cite_note-usp-ch6-p153-72) The [command-line](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface") syntax is `alpha | bravo`. `alpha` will write to the pipe when its computation is ready and then sleep in the wait queue.[[71]](#cite_note-usp-ch6-p148-73) `bravo` will then be moved to the [ready queue](/wiki/Multilevel_feedback_queue "Multilevel feedback queue") and soon will read from its input stream.[[72]](#cite_note-usp-ch6-p149-74) The kernel will generate *software interrupts* to coordinate the piping.[[72]](#cite_note-usp-ch6-p149-74)

title: Operating system
text:
##### Hardware interrupt

[Input/output](/wiki/Input/output "Input/output") (I/O) [devices](/wiki/Peripheral "Peripheral") are slower than the CPU. Therefore, it would slow down the computer if the CPU had to [wait](/wiki/Busy_waiting "Busy waiting") for each I/O to finish. Instead, a computer may implement interrupts for I/O completion, avoiding the need for [polling](/wiki/Polling_(computer_science) "Polling (computer science)") or busy waiting.[[73]](#cite_note-sco-ch5-p292-75)

Some computers require an interrupt for each character or word, costing a significant amount of CPU time. [Direct memory access](/wiki/Direct_memory_access "Direct memory access") (DMA) is an architecture feature to allow devices to bypass the CPU and access [main memory](/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") directly.[[74]](#cite_note-A22-6821-7-storage-76) (Separate from the architecture, a device may perform direct memory access[[c]](#cite_note-77) to and from main memory either directly or via a bus.)[[75]](#cite_note-sco-ch5-p294-78)[[d]](#cite_note-79)

When a [computer user](/wiki/User_(computing) "User (computing)") types a key on the keyboard, typically the character appears immediately on the screen. Likewise, when a user moves a [mouse](/wiki/Computer_mouse "Computer mouse"), the [cursor](/wiki/Cursor_(user_interface) "Cursor (user interface)") immediately moves across the screen. Each keystroke and mouse movement generates an *interrupt* called *Interrupt-driven I/O*. An interrupt-driven I/O occurs when a process causes an interrupt for every character[[75]](#cite_note-sco-ch5-p294-78) or word[[76]](#cite_note-80) transmitted.
