title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Three basic distributions

To better illustrate this point, examine three system [architectures](/wiki/Software_architecture "Software architecture"); centralized, decentralized, and distributed. In this examination, consider three structural aspects: organization, connection, and control. Organization describes a system's physical arrangement characteristics. Connection covers the communication pathways among nodes. Control manages the operation of the earlier two considerations.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
#### Organization

A [centralized system](/wiki/Centralized_computing "Centralized computing") has one level of structure, where all constituent elements directly depend upon a single control element. A [decentralized system](/wiki/Decentralized_system "Decentralized system") is hierarchical. The bottom level unites subsets of a system's entities. These entity subsets in turn combine at higher levels, ultimately culminating at a central master element. A distributed system is a collection of autonomous elements with no concept of levels.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
#### Connection

Centralized systems connect constituents directly to a central master entity in a hub and spoke fashion. A decentralized system (aka [network system](/wiki/Network_operating_system "Network operating system")) incorporates direct and indirect paths between constituent elements and the central entity. Typically this is configured as a hierarchy with only one shortest path between any two elements. Finally, the distributed operating system requires no pattern; direct and indirect connections are possible between any two elements. Consider the 1970s phenomena of “[string art](/wiki/String_art "String art")” or a [spirograph](/wiki/Spirograph "Spirograph") drawing as a [fully connected system](/wiki/Fully_connected_network "Fully connected network"), and the [spider's web](/wiki/Spider_web "Spider web") or the [Interstate Highway System](/wiki/Interstate_Highway_System "Interstate Highway System") between U.S. cities as examples of a *partially connected system*.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
#### Control

Centralized and decentralized systems have directed [flows of connection](/wiki/Software_flow_control "Software flow control") to and from the central entity, while distributed systems communicate along arbitrary paths. This is the pivotal notion of the third consideration. Control involves allocating tasks and data to system elements balancing efficiency, responsiveness, and complexity.

Centralized and decentralized systems offer more control, potentially easing administration by limiting options. Distributed systems are more difficult to explicitly control, but scale better horizontally and offer fewer points of system-wide failure. The associations conform to the needs imposed by its design but not by organizational chaos

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Transparency

*Transparency* or *single-system image* refers to the ability of an application to treat the system on which it operates without regard to whether it is distributed and without regard to hardware or other implementation details. Many areas of a system can benefit from transparency, including access, location, performance, naming, and migration. The consideration of transparency directly affects decision making in every aspect of design of a distributed operating system. Transparency can impose certain requirements and/or restrictions on other design considerations.

Systems can optionally violate transparency to varying degrees to meet specific application requirements. For example, a distributed operating system may present a hard drive on one computer as "C:" and a drive on another computer as "G:". The user does not require any knowledge of device drivers or the drive's location; both devices work the same way, from the application's perspective. A less transparent interface might require the application to know which computer hosts the drive. Transparency domains:
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
Systems can optionally violate transparency to varying degrees to meet specific application requirements. For example, a distributed operating system may present a hard drive on one computer as "C:" and a drive on another computer as "G:". The user does not require any knowledge of device drivers or the drive's location; both devices work the same way, from the application's perspective. A less transparent interface might require the application to know which computer hosts the drive. Transparency domains:

- *Location transparency* – Location transparency comprises two distinct aspects of transparency, naming transparency and user mobility. Naming transparency requires that nothing in the physical or logical references to any system entity should expose any indication of the entity's location, or its local or remote relationship to the user or application. User mobility requires the consistent referencing of system entities, regardless of the system location from which the reference originates.[[8]](#cite_note-Sinha1997-8): 20
- *Access transparency* – Local and remote system entities must remain indistinguishable when viewed through the user interface. The distributed operating system maintains this perception through the exposure of a single access mechanism for a system entity, regardless of that entity being local or remote to the user. Transparency dictates that any differences in methods of accessing any particular system entity—either local or remote—must be both invisible to, and undetectable by the user.[[3]](#cite_note-Gościński1991-3): 84
- *Migration transparency* – Resources and activities migrate from one element to another controlled solely by the system and without user/application knowledge or action.[[36]](#cite_note-Galli2000-36): 16
- *Replication transparency* – The process or fact that a resource has been duplicated on another element occurs under system control and without user/application knowledge or intervention.[[36]](#cite_note-Galli2000-36): 16
- *Concurrency transparency* – Users/applications are unaware of and unaffected by the presence/activities of other users.[[36]](#cite_note-Galli2000-36): 16
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
- *Failure transparency* – The system is responsible for detection and remediation of system failures. No user knowledge/action is involved other than waiting for the system to resolve the problem.[[9]](#cite_note-Chow1997-9): 30
- *Performance Transparency* – The system is responsible for the detection and remediation of local or global performance shortfalls. Note that system policies may prefer some users/user classes/tasks over others. No user knowledge or interaction. is involved.[[8]](#cite_note-Sinha1997-8): 23
- *Size/Scale transparency* – The system is responsible for managing its geographic reach, number of nodes, level of node capability without any required user knowledge or interaction.[[8]](#cite_note-Sinha1997-8): 23
- *Revision transparency* – The system is responsible for upgrades and revisions and changes to system infrastructure without user knowledge or action.[[9]](#cite_note-Chow1997-9): 30
- *Control transparency* – The system is responsible for providing all system information, constants, properties, configuration settings, etc. in a consistent appearance, connotation, and denotation to all users and applications.[[3]](#cite_note-Gościński1991-3): 84
- *Data transparency* – The system is responsible for providing data to applications without user knowledge or action relating to where the system stores it.[[3]](#cite_note-Gościński1991-3): 85
- *Parallelism transparency* – The system is responsible for exploiting any ability to parallelize task execution without user knowledge or interaction. Arguably the most difficult aspect of transparency, and described by Tanenbaum as the "Holy grail" for distributed system designers.[[37]](#cite_note-Tanenbaum1995-37): 23–25
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Inter-process communication

[Inter-Process Communication](/wiki/Inter-Process_Communication "Inter-Process Communication") (IPC) is the implementation of general communication, process interaction, and [dataflow](/wiki/Dataflow "Dataflow") between [threads](/wiki/Thread_(computer_science) "Thread (computer science)") and/or [processes](/wiki/Process_(computing) "Process (computing)") both within a node, and between nodes in a distributed OS. The intra-node and inter-node communication requirements drive low-level IPC design, which is the typical approach to implementing communication functions that support transparency. In this sense, Interprocess communication is the greatest underlying concept in the low-level design considerations of a distributed operating system.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Process management

[Process management](/wiki/Process_management_(computing) "Process management (computing)") provides policies and mechanisms for effective and efficient sharing of resources between distributed processes. These policies and mechanisms support operations involving the allocation and de-allocation of processes and ports to processors, as well as mechanisms to run, suspend, migrate, halt, or resume process execution. While these resources and operations can be either local or remote with respect to each other, the distributed OS maintains state and synchronization over all processes in the system.

As an example, [load balancing](/wiki/Load_balancing_(computing) "Load balancing (computing)") is a common process management function. Load balancing monitors node performance and is responsible for shifting activity across nodes when the system is out of balance. One load balancing function is picking a process to move. The kernel may employ several selection mechanisms, including priority-based choice. This mechanism chooses a process based on a policy such as 'newest request'. The system implements the policy
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Resource management

[Systems resources](/wiki/Resource_(computer_science) "Resource (computer science)") such as memory, files, devices, etc. are distributed throughout a system, and at any given moment, any of these nodes may have light to idle workloads. *Load sharing* and load balancing require many policy-oriented decisions, ranging from finding idle CPUs, when to move, and which to move. Many [algorithms](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm") exist to aid in these decisions; however, this calls for a second level of decision making policy in choosing the algorithm best suited for the scenario, and the conditions surrounding the scenario.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Reliability

Distributed OS can provide the necessary resources and services to achieve high levels of *reliability*, or the ability to prevent and/or recover from errors. [Faults](/wiki/Fault_(technology) "Fault (technology)") are physical or logical defects that can cause errors in the system. For a system to be reliable, it must somehow overcome the adverse effects of faults.

The primary methods for dealing with faults include *fault avoidance*, [fault tolerance](/wiki/Fault-tolerant_design "Fault-tolerant design"), and *fault detection and recovery*. Fault avoidance covers proactive measures taken to minimize the occurrence of faults. These proactive measures can be in the form of *[transactions](/wiki/Transaction_processing "Transaction processing")*, [replication](/wiki/Replication_(computer_science) "Replication (computer science)") and [backups](/wiki/Replication_(computer_science)#Primary-backup_and_multi-primary_replication "Replication (computer science)"). Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to continue operation in the presence of a fault. In the event, the system should detect and recover full functionality. In any event, any actions taken should make every effort to preserve the *single system image*.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Availability

[Availability](/wiki/Availability "Availability") is the fraction of time during which the system can respond to requests.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Performance

Many [benchmark metrics](/wiki/Benchmark_(computing) "Benchmark (computing)") quantify [performance](/wiki/Computer_performance "Computer performance"); throughput, response time, job completions per unit time, system utilization, etc. With respect to a distributed OS, performance most often distills to a balance between [process parallelism](/wiki/Parallel_computing "Parallel computing") and IPC.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Managing the [task granularity](/wiki/Granularity#In_computing "Granularity") of parallelism in a sensible relation to the messages required for support is extremely effective.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Also, identifying when it is more beneficial to [migrate a process](/wiki/Process_migration "Process migration") to its data, rather than copy the data, is effective as well.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Synchronization

Cooperating [concurrent processes](/wiki/Concurrent_computing "Concurrent computing") have an inherent need for [synchronization](/wiki/Synchronization_(computer_science) "Synchronization (computer science)"), which ensures that changes happen in a correct and predictable fashion. Three basic situations that define the scope of this need:

:   - one or more processes must synchronize at a given point for one or more other processes to continue,

- one or more processes must wait for an asynchronous condition in order to continue,
    - or a process must establish exclusive access to a shared resource.

Improper synchronization can lead to multiple failure modes including loss of [atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability](/wiki/ACID "ACID"), [deadlock](/wiki/Deadlock_(computer_science) "Deadlock (computer science)"), [livelock](/wiki/Livelock "Livelock") and loss of [serializability](/wiki/Serializability "Serializability").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Distributed operating system

title: Distributed operating system
text:
### Flexibility

[Flexibility](/wiki/Flexibility_(engineering) "Flexibility (engineering)") in a distributed operating system is enhanced through the modular characteristics of the distributed OS, and by providing a richer set of higher-level services. The completeness and quality of the kernel/microkernel simplifies implementation of such services, and potentially enables service providers greater choice of providers for such services.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Dispersed operating system computing

Dispersed operating system computing (DOSC) is a computing paradigm that implements application software via "application objects" that have embedded operating system functionality. Example implementations include web servers,[[47]](#cite_note-47) VoIP,[[48]](#cite_note-48) and [file systems](/wiki/File_system "File system").[[49]](#cite_note-49)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
**[RISC OS](/wiki/RISC_OS "RISC OS")**, the computer [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") developed by [Acorn Computers](/wiki/Acorn_Computers "Acorn Computers") for their [ARM](/wiki/ARM_architecture "ARM architecture")-based [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") range, was originally released in 1987 as *Arthur 0.20*, and soon followed by *Arthur 0.30*, and *Arthur 1.20*. The next version, *Arthur 2*, became *RISC OS 2* and was completed in September 1988 and made available in April 1989. *RISC OS 3* was released with the very earliest version of the A5000 in 1991 and contained a series of new features. By 1996 RISC OS had been shipped on over 500,000 systems.[[1]](#cite_note-chrisacorns-1)

*RISC OS 4* was released by [RISCOS Ltd](/wiki/RISCOS_Ltd "RISCOS Ltd") (ROL) in July 1999, based on the continued development of OS 3.8. ROL had in March 1999 licensed the rights to RISC OS from Element 14 (the renamed Acorn) and eventually from the new owner, [Pace Micro Technology](/wiki/Pace_Micro_Technology "Pace Micro Technology"). According to the company, over 6,400 copies of OS 4.02 on ROM were sold up until production was ceased in mid-2005.

title: History of RISC OS
text:
*RISC OS 4* was released by [RISCOS Ltd](/wiki/RISCOS_Ltd "RISCOS Ltd") (ROL) in July 1999, based on the continued development of OS 3.8. ROL had in March 1999 licensed the rights to RISC OS from Element 14 (the renamed Acorn) and eventually from the new owner, [Pace Micro Technology](/wiki/Pace_Micro_Technology "Pace Micro Technology"). According to the company, over 6,400 copies of OS 4.02 on ROM were sold up until production was ceased in mid-2005.

*RISC OS Select* was launched in May 2001 by ROL. This is a subscription scheme allowing users access to the latest OS updates. These upgrades are released as soft-loadable [ROM images](/wiki/ROM_image "ROM image"), separate to the ROM where the boot OS is stored, and are loaded at boot time. *Select 1* was shipped in May 2002, with *Select 2* following in November 2002 and the final release of *Select 3* in June 2004. ROL released the ROM based OS 4.39 the same month, dubbed *RISC OS Adjust* as a play on the RISC OS GUI convention of calling the three mouse buttons 'Select', 'Menu' and 'Adjust'. ROL sold its 500th Adjust ROM in early 2006.

title: History of RISC OS

*RISC OS Select* was launched in May 2001 by ROL. This is a subscription scheme allowing users access to the latest OS updates. These upgrades are released as soft-loadable [ROM images](/wiki/ROM_image "ROM image"), separate to the ROM where the boot OS is stored, and are loaded at boot time. *Select 1* was shipped in May 2002, with *Select 2* following in November 2002 and the final release of *Select 3* in June 2004. ROL released the ROM based OS 4.39 the same month, dubbed *RISC OS Adjust* as a play on the RISC OS GUI convention of calling the three mouse buttons 'Select', 'Menu' and 'Adjust'. ROL sold its 500th Adjust ROM in early 2006.

*RISC OS 5* was released in October 2002 on [Castle Technology](/wiki/Castle_Technology "Castle Technology")'s *Acorn clone* [Iyonix PC](/wiki/Iyonix_PC "Iyonix PC"). OS 5 is a separate evolution based upon the [NCOS](/wiki/NCOS "NCOS") work done by Pace for [set-top boxes](/wiki/Set-top_box "Set-top box"). In October 2006, Castle announced a source sharing license plan for elements of OS 5. This Shared Source Initiative (SSI) is managed by [RISC OS Open Ltd](/wiki/RISC_OS_Open_Ltd "RISC OS Open Ltd") (ROOL). RISC OS 5 has since been released under a fully [free and open source](/wiki/Free_and_open_source "Free and open source") [Apache 2.0 license](/wiki/Apache_license "Apache license"), while the older no longer maintained RISC OS 6 has not.

*RISC OS 5* was released in October 2002 on [Castle Technology](/wiki/Castle_Technology "Castle Technology")'s *Acorn clone* [Iyonix PC](/wiki/Iyonix_PC "Iyonix PC"). OS 5 is a separate evolution based upon the [NCOS](/wiki/NCOS "NCOS") work done by Pace for [set-top boxes](/wiki/Set-top_box "Set-top box"). In October 2006, Castle announced a source sharing license plan for elements of OS 5. This Shared Source Initiative (SSI) is managed by [RISC OS Open Ltd](/wiki/RISC_OS_Open_Ltd "RISC OS Open Ltd") (ROOL). RISC OS 5 has since been released under a fully [free and open source](/wiki/Free_and_open_source "Free and open source") [Apache 2.0 license](/wiki/Apache_license "Apache license"), while the older no longer maintained RISC OS 6 has not.

*RISC OS Six* was also announced in October 2006 by ROL. This is the next generation of their stream of the operating system. The first product to be launched under the name was the continuation of the Select scheme, *Select 4*. A beta-version of OS 6, Preview 1 (*Select 4i1*), was available in 2007 as a free download to all subscribers to the Select scheme, while in April 2009 the final release of *Select 5* was shipped. The latest release of RISC OS from ROL is *Select 6i1*, shipped in December 2009.

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The OS was designed in the [United Kingdom](/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") by [Acorn](/wiki/Acorn_Computers_Ltd "Acorn Computers Ltd") for the [32-bit](/wiki/32-bit "32-bit") ARM based [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes"), and released in its first version in 1987, as the [Arthur](/wiki/Arthur_(operating_system) "Arthur (operating system)") operating system.
The first public release of the OS was *Arthur 1.20* in June 1987.[[2]](#cite_note-History310-2)

It was bundled with a desktop [graphical user interface](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") (GUI), which mostly comprises [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language") software modules,[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] and the Desktop module itself being written in [BBC BASIC](/wiki/BBC_BASIC "BBC BASIC").[[3]](#cite_note-pcw_1987-3) It features a colour-scheme typically described as "[technicolor](/wiki/Technicolor "Technicolor")".[[4]](#cite_note-osnewsDock-4)

The graphical desktop runs on top of a [command-line](/wiki/Command_line_interface "Command line interface") driven operating system which owes much to Acorn's earlier [MOS](/wiki/Acorn_MOS "Acorn MOS") operating system for its [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro") range of [8-bit](/wiki/8-bit "8-bit") microcomputers.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The graphical desktop runs on top of a [command-line](/wiki/Command_line_interface "Command line interface") driven operating system which owes much to Acorn's earlier [MOS](/wiki/Acorn_MOS "Acorn MOS") operating system for its [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro") range of [8-bit](/wiki/8-bit "8-bit") microcomputers.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5)

Arthur, as originally conceived, was intended to deliver similar functionality to the operating system for the [BBC Master](/wiki/BBC_Master "BBC Master") series of computers, [MOS](/wiki/Acorn_MOS "Acorn MOS"), as a reaction to the fact that a more advanced operating system research project ([ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)")) would not be ready in time for the [Archimedes](/wiki/Archimedes_(computer) "Archimedes (computer)").[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5)

The Arthur project team, led by Paul Fellows, was given just five months to develop it entirely from the ground up—with the directive "just make it like the BBC micro". It was intended as a stop-gap until the operating system which Acorn had under development ([ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)")) could be completed. However, the latter was delayed time and again, and was eventually dropped when it became apparent that the Arthur development could be extended to have a window manager and full desktop environment. Also, it was small enough to run on the first 512K machines with only a floppy disc, whereas ARX required 4 megabytes and a hard drive.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Also, it was small enough to run on the first 512K machines with only a floppy disc, whereas ARX required 4 megabytes and a hard drive.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The OS development was carried out using a prototype ARM-based system connected to a BBC computer, before moving onto the prototype [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") the A500.[[6]](#cite_note-chrisacornsA500-6)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The OS development was carried out using a prototype ARM-based system connected to a BBC computer, before moving onto the prototype [Acorn Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") the A500.[[6]](#cite_note-chrisacornsA500-6)

Arthur was not a multitasking operating system, but offered support for adding application-level [cooperative multitasking](/wiki/Cooperative_multitasking "Cooperative multitasking").[[7]](#cite_note-pountain198710-7) No other version of the operating system was released externally, but internally the development of the desktop and window management continued, with the addition of a cooperative multitasking system, implemented by Neil Raine, which used the memory management hardware to swap-out one task, and bring in another between call-and-return from the `Wimp_Poll` call that applications were obliged to make to get messages under the desktop. Reminiscent of a similar technique employed by [MultiFinder](/wiki/MultiFinder "MultiFinder") on the [Apple Macintosh](/wiki/Apple_Macintosh "Apple Macintosh"),[[8]](#cite_note-byte198711-8) this transformed a single-application-at-a-time system into one that could operate a full multi-tasking desktop. This transformation took place at version 1.6 though it was not made public until released, with the name change from Arthur to RISC OS, as version 2.0.[[9]](#cite_note-fellows-9)

Most software made for Arthur 1.2 can be run under RISC OS 2 and later because, underneath the desktop, the original Arthur OS core, API interfaces and modular structures remain as the heart of all versions. (A few titles will not work, however, because they used undocumented features, side effects or in a few cases APIs that became deprecated).[*[original research?](/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research "Wikipedia:No original research")*]

## RISC OS 2

RISC OS was a rapid development of Arthur 1.2 after the failure of the [ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)") project.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5) Given growing dissatisfaction with various bugs and limitations with Arthur, testing of what was then known as Arthur 2 was apparently ongoing during 1988 with selected software houses.[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
RISC OS was a rapid development of Arthur 1.2 after the failure of the [ARX](/wiki/ARX_(operating_system) "ARX (operating system)") project.[[5]](#cite_note-acornpov-5) Given growing dissatisfaction with various bugs and limitations with Arthur, testing of what was then known as Arthur 2 was apparently ongoing during 1988 with selected software houses.[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11)

At this stage, Computer Concepts, who had been prolific developers for the BBC Micro and who had begun software development for the Archimedes, had already initiated a rival operating system project, Impulse, to support their own applications (including the desktop publishing application that would eventually become [Impression](/wiki/Impression_(software) "Impression (software)")), stating that Arthur did not meet the "hundreds of requirements" involved including "true multi-tasking".[[12]](#cite_note-acornuser198806-12) Such an operating system was to be offered free of charge with the planned application packages,[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11) but with the release of RISC OS and Computer Concepts acknowledging that RISC OS "overcomes the old problems with Arthur", the applications were to be able to run under either RISC OS or Impulse.[[13]](#cite_note-acornuser198901-13) Impression was eventually released as a RISC OS application.[[14]](#cite_note-acornuser199005-14)

Ultimately, Arthur 2 was renamed to *RISC OS*, and was first sold as *RISC OS 2.00* in April 1989.[[15]](#cite_note-acornuser198902-15)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
At this stage, Computer Concepts, who had been prolific developers for the BBC Micro and who had begun software development for the Archimedes, had already initiated a rival operating system project, Impulse, to support their own applications (including the desktop publishing application that would eventually become [Impression](/wiki/Impression_(software) "Impression (software)")), stating that Arthur did not meet the "hundreds of requirements" involved including "true multi-tasking".[[12]](#cite_note-acornuser198806-12) Such an operating system was to be offered free of charge with the planned application packages,[[11]](#cite_note-acornuser198807-11) but with the release of RISC OS and Computer Concepts acknowledging that RISC OS "overcomes the old problems with Arthur", the applications were to be able to run under either RISC OS or Impulse.[[13]](#cite_note-acornuser198901-13) Impression was eventually released as a RISC OS application.[[14]](#cite_note-acornuser199005-14)

Ultimately, Arthur 2 was renamed to *RISC OS*, and was first sold as *RISC OS 2.00* in April 1989.[[15]](#cite_note-acornuser198902-15)

The operating system implements [co-operative multitasking](/wiki/Co-operative_multitasking "Co-operative multitasking") with some limitations but is not [multi-threaded](/wiki/Thread_(computer_science) "Thread (computer science)"). It uses the [ADFS](/wiki/Advanced_Disc_Filing_System "Advanced Disc Filing System") file system for both floppy and hard disc access. It ran from a 512 [KB](/wiki/Kilobyte "Kilobyte") set of [ROMs](/wiki/Read-only_memory "Read-only memory"). The [WIMP](/wiki/WIMP_(computing) "WIMP (computing)") interface offers all the standard features and fixes many of the [bugs](/wiki/Computer_bug "Computer bug") that had hindered Arthur. It lacks [virtual memory](/wiki/Virtual_memory "Virtual memory") and extensive [memory protection](/wiki/Memory_protection "Memory protection") (applications are protected from each other, but many functions have to be implemented as 'modules' which have full access to the memory). At the time of release, the main advantage of the OS was its ROM; it booted very quickly and while it was easy to crash, it was impossible to permanently break the OS from software. Its high performance was due to much of the system being written in [ARM](/wiki/ARM_architecture "ARM architecture") [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The operating system implements [co-operative multitasking](/wiki/Co-operative_multitasking "Co-operative multitasking") with some limitations but is not [multi-threaded](/wiki/Thread_(computer_science) "Thread (computer science)"). It uses the [ADFS](/wiki/Advanced_Disc_Filing_System "Advanced Disc Filing System") file system for both floppy and hard disc access. It ran from a 512 [KB](/wiki/Kilobyte "Kilobyte") set of [ROMs](/wiki/Read-only_memory "Read-only memory"). The [WIMP](/wiki/WIMP_(computing) "WIMP (computing)") interface offers all the standard features and fixes many of the [bugs](/wiki/Computer_bug "Computer bug") that had hindered Arthur. It lacks [virtual memory](/wiki/Virtual_memory "Virtual memory") and extensive [memory protection](/wiki/Memory_protection "Memory protection") (applications are protected from each other, but many functions have to be implemented as 'modules' which have full access to the memory). At the time of release, the main advantage of the OS was its ROM; it booted very quickly and while it was easy to crash, it was impossible to permanently break the OS from software. Its high performance was due to much of the system being written in [ARM](/wiki/ARM_architecture "ARM architecture") [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The OS was designed with users in mind, rather than OS designers.[[16]](#cite_note-Stoye1990-16) It is organised as a relatively small kernel which defines a standard software interface to which extension modules are required to conform. Much of the system's functionality is implemented in modules coded in the ROM, though these can be supplanted by more evolved versions loaded into [RAM](/wiki/Random_Access_Memory "Random Access Memory"). Among the kernel facilities are a general mechanism, named the callback handler, which allows a supervisor module to perform process multiplexing. This facility is used by a module forming part of the standard editor program to provide a [terminal emulator](/wiki/Terminal_emulator "Terminal emulator") window for console applications. The same approach made it possible for advanced users to implement modules giving RISC OS the ability to do [pre-emptive multitasking](/wiki/Pre-emptive_multitasking "Pre-emptive multitasking").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: History of RISC OS
text:
## RISC OS 3

RISC OS 3 introduced a number of new features,[[18]](#cite_note-RO3MarketingQandA-18) including multitasking *Filer* operations, applications and fonts in ROM, no limit on number of open windows, ability to move windows off screen, safe [shutdown](/wiki/Shutdown_(computing) "Shutdown (computing)"), the *Pinboard*, grouping of icon bar icons, up to 128 tasks, native ability to read [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") format discs and use named hard discs. Improved [configuration](/wiki/Configuration_file "Configuration file") was also included, by way of multiple windows to change the settings.[[18]](#cite_note-RO3MarketingQandA-18)

*RISC OS 3.00* was released with the very earliest version of the A5000 in 1991; it is almost four times the size of RISC OS 2 and runs from a 2 [MB](/wiki/Mebibyte "Mebibyte") ROM. It improves multitasking and also places some of the more popular base applications in the ROM. RISC OS 3.00 had several bugs and was replaced by RISC OS 3.1 a few months later; the upgraded ROMs were supplied for the cost of postage.

*RISC OS 3.00* was released with the very earliest version of the A5000 in 1991; it is almost four times the size of RISC OS 2 and runs from a 2 [MB](/wiki/Mebibyte "Mebibyte") ROM. It improves multitasking and also places some of the more popular base applications in the ROM. RISC OS 3.00 had several bugs and was replaced by RISC OS 3.1 a few months later; the upgraded ROMs were supplied for the cost of postage.

*RISC OS 3.1* was released later and sold built into the A3010, A3020, A4000, A4 and later A5000 models. It was also made available as replacement ROMs for the A5000 and earlier [Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") machines (this is the last RISC OS version suitable for those machines). Three variants were released: *RISC OS 3.10* the base version, *RISC OS 3.11* which included a slight update that fixes some serial port issues and *RISC OS 3.19* which was a German translation.

title: History of RISC OS
text:
*RISC OS 3.1* was released later and sold built into the A3010, A3020, A4000, A4 and later A5000 models. It was also made available as replacement ROMs for the A5000 and earlier [Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") machines (this is the last RISC OS version suitable for those machines). Three variants were released: *RISC OS 3.10* the base version, *RISC OS 3.11* which included a slight update that fixes some serial port issues and *RISC OS 3.19* which was a German translation.

*RISC OS 3.50* was sold from 1994 with the first [Risc PCs](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC"). Due to the very different hardware architecture of the [Risc PC](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC"), including an ARM 6 processor, 16- and 24-bit colour and a different IO chip (IOMD), RISC OS 3.50 was not made available for the older [Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") and A Series ARM2 and 3 machines. RISC OS 3.5 was somewhat shoehorned into the 2 MB footprint, and moved the ROM applications of RISC OS 3.1 onto the hard drive; this proved so unpopular that they were later moved back into ROM. This version introduced issues of [backward compatibility](/wiki/Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility"), particularly with [games](/wiki/Computer_game "Computer game").

title: History of RISC OS
text:
*RISC OS 3.50* was sold from 1994 with the first [Risc PCs](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC"). Due to the very different hardware architecture of the [Risc PC](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC"), including an ARM 6 processor, 16- and 24-bit colour and a different IO chip (IOMD), RISC OS 3.50 was not made available for the older [Archimedes](/wiki/Acorn_Archimedes "Acorn Archimedes") and A Series ARM2 and 3 machines. RISC OS 3.5 was somewhat shoehorned into the 2 MB footprint, and moved the ROM applications of RISC OS 3.1 onto the hard drive; this proved so unpopular that they were later moved back into ROM. This version introduced issues of [backward compatibility](/wiki/Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility"), particularly with [games](/wiki/Computer_game "Computer game").

*RISC OS 3.60* followed in 1995. The OS features much improved [hard disk](/wiki/Hard_disk "Hard disk") access and its [networking](/wiki/Computer_network "Computer network") was enhanced to include [TCP/IP](/wiki/TCP/IP "TCP/IP") as standard in addition to Acorn's existing proprietary [Econet](/wiki/Econet "Econet") system. The hardware support was also improved; [Risc PCs](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC") could now use ARM7 processors. Acorn's [A7000](/wiki/Acorn_A7000 "Acorn A7000") machine with its ARM7500 processor was also supported. RISC OS 3.6 was twice the size of RISC OS 3.5, shipping on 4 MB in two ROM chips; components that had been moved onto disk in 3.5 (the standard application suite and networking) were now moved back into ROM.[[19]](#cite_note-riscos.com-19)

The hardware support was also improved; [Risc PCs](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC") could now use ARM7 processors. Acorn's [A7000](/wiki/Acorn_A7000 "Acorn A7000") machine with its ARM7500 processor was also supported. RISC OS 3.6 was twice the size of RISC OS 3.5, shipping on 4 MB in two ROM chips; components that had been moved onto disk in 3.5 (the standard application suite and networking) were now moved back into ROM.[[19]](#cite_note-riscos.com-19)

*RISC OS 3.70* was released in 1996. The primary changes in the OS was support for the [StrongARM](/wiki/StrongARM "StrongARM") processor that was made available as an upgrade for the [Risc PC](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC"). This required extensive code changes due to [StrongARM's](/wiki/StrongARM "StrongARM") split data and instruction cache ([Harvard architecture](/wiki/Harvard_architecture "Harvard architecture")) and 32-bit interrupt modes.

*RISC OS 3.71* is a small update released to support the hardware in the Acorn [A7000+](/wiki/Acorn_A7000 "Acorn A7000") with its ARM7500FE processor. The FE offered hardware support for floating point mathematics, which until then was usually emulated in one of the RISC OS Software modules).

title: History of RISC OS
text:
## Demise of Acorn Computers Ltd

Acorn officially halted work in all areas except [set-top boxes](/wiki/Set-top_box "Set-top box") in January 1999 and the company was renamed [Element 14](/wiki/Element_14_(company) "Element 14 (company)")[[21]](#cite_note-Companies_House_"Acorn_Computers_Limited"-21) (the 14th element of the [periodic table](/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") being [silicon](/wiki/Silicon "Silicon")) with a new goal to become purely a Silicon design business (like the previous very successful spin off of ARM from Acorn in 1990). RISC OS development was halted during the development of OS 4.0 for the RiscPC 2 ("[Phoebe 2100](/wiki/Phoebe_2100 "Phoebe 2100")"), whose completion was also cancelled. A beta version, OS 3.8 ("Ursula") for the original RiscPC, had previously been released to developers. The project code names of Phoebe (for the hardware), Ursula (for the software) and Chandler (for the graphics processor chip) were taken from the names of characters in the TV series *[Friends](/wiki/Friends "Friends")* (Phoebe and Ursula were twin sisters in the series).

title: History of RISC OS
text:
Acorn officially halted work in all areas except [set-top boxes](/wiki/Set-top_box "Set-top box") in January 1999 and the company was renamed [Element 14](/wiki/Element_14_(company) "Element 14 (company)")[[21]](#cite_note-Companies_House_"Acorn_Computers_Limited"-21) (the 14th element of the [periodic table](/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table") being [silicon](/wiki/Silicon "Silicon")) with a new goal to become purely a Silicon design business (like the previous very successful spin off of ARM from Acorn in 1990). RISC OS development was halted during the development of OS 4.0 for the RiscPC 2 ("[Phoebe 2100](/wiki/Phoebe_2100 "Phoebe 2100")"), whose completion was also cancelled. A beta version, OS 3.8 ("Ursula") for the original RiscPC, had previously been released to developers. The project code names of Phoebe (for the hardware), Ursula (for the software) and Chandler (for the graphics processor chip) were taken from the names of characters in the TV series *[Friends](/wiki/Friends "Friends")* (Phoebe and Ursula were twin sisters in the series).

This led to a number of rescue efforts to try to keep the Acorn desktop computer business alive. Acorn held discussions with many interested parties, and eventually agreed to exclusively licence RISC OS to RISCOS Ltd, which was formed from a consortium of dealers, developers and end-users. Pace purchased the rights to use and develop NCOS.
There were also a number of projects to bring the advantages of the RISC Operating System to other platforms by the creation of the [ROX Desktop](/wiki/ROX_Desktop "ROX Desktop") to provide a RISC OS-like interface on [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") and [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") systems. The separate work by RISC OS Ltd and Pace resulted in a [code fork](/wiki/Code_fork "Code fork"). This continued after the subsequent licensing agreement with Castle Technology, causing much community debate at the time.[[22]](#cite_note-osnews_what_it_would_take-22) The debate remains ongoing in 2011.

title: History of RISC OS
text: ## Work post-Acorn by RISCOS Ltd
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > History of RISC OS

title: History of RISC OS
text:
### RISC OS 4

In March 1999, a new company called [RISCOS Ltd](/wiki/RISCOS_Ltd "RISCOS Ltd") was founded. They licensed the rights to RISC OS from Element 14 (and eventually from the new owner, [Pace Micro Technology](/wiki/Pace_Micro_Technology "Pace Micro Technology"))[[23]](#cite_note-riscos.com-1999-23) and continued the development of OS 3.8, releasing it as *RISC OS 4* in July 1999.[[24]](#cite_note-riscos.com-1999-2-24)

Whilst the hardware support for Phoebe was not needed, the core improvements to RISC OS 3.80 could be finished and released. They included:

- a better file system, increasing the number of items in directory from 77 to approximately 88,000 and increasing the max length of a filename from 10 characters to 255[[25]](#cite_note-iconbar.com-1999-25)[[26]](#cite_note-marutan-26)
- a plugin based system configuration utility[[27]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-27)
- a new screensaver API[[28]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-2-28)
- an enhanced window manager[[29]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-3-29)
- an updated interactive help application[[30]](#cite_note-marutan-wiki-4-30)
- a redesigned set of icons

According to the company, over 6,400 copies of RISC OS 4.02 on ROM were sold up until production was ceased in mid-2005.[[31]](#cite_note-riscos.com2005oct-31)

According to the company, over 6,400 copies of RISC OS 4.02 on ROM were sold up until production was ceased in mid-2005.[[31]](#cite_note-riscos.com2005oct-31)

During 1999 and 2000, RISCOS Ltd also released versions of RISC OS 4 to support several additional hardware platforms, the [MicroDigital Mico](/w/index.php?title=MicroDigital_Mico&action=edit&redlink=1 "MicroDigital Mico (page does not exist)"),[[32]](#cite_note-chrisacorns1999-32) [MicroDigital Omega](/wiki/MicroDigital_Omega "MicroDigital Omega"), [RiscStation R7500](/w/index.php?title=RiscStation_R7500&action=edit&redlink=1 "RiscStation R7500 (page does not exist)")[[33]](#cite_note-chriswhyRiscStation-33) and the Castle Kinetic RiscPC.[[34]](#cite_note-iconbar.comKinetic-34) In 2003 a version of RISC OS 4 was released with support for the Millipede Graphics AlphaLock podule.[[35]](#cite_note-riscos.comRO4-35)

RISC OS 4 is also available for various hardware emulators for other operating systems. In September 2003 [VirtualAcorn](/wiki/VirtualAcorn "VirtualAcorn") released the commercial emulator [VirtualRPC](/wiki/VirtualAcorn "VirtualAcorn") which included a copy of RISC OS 4.02.[[36]](#cite_note-riscos.comVirtualAcorn-36) In December 2008 RISCOS Ltd made 4.02 available for non-commercial emulators for £5 in a product called Virtually Free.[[37]](#cite_note-riscos.comRO402-37)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
### RISC OS Select and Adjust

In May 2001, the company launched *RISC OS Select*, a subscription scheme allowing users access to the latest OS updates. These upgrades are released as soft-loadable [ROM images](/wiki/ROM_image "ROM image"), separate to the ROM where the boot OS is stored, and are loaded at boot time.[[38]](#cite_note-riscos.comSelect-38) By providing soft-loads, physical ROM costs are eliminated and updates are able to be delivered with accelerated speed and frequency.[[39]](#cite_note-ROL_Select-39) It has also allowed the company to subsidise the retail price of ROM releases, which are generally a culmination of the last few Select upgrades with a few extra minor changes.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In May 2002 the final release of Select 1 was shipped that included;[[40]](#cite_note-riscos.comSelectCD-40)

- [DHCP](/wiki/DHCP "DHCP") client
- Multi-User support and logon
- Preview versions of new printer support and networking with [AppleTalk](/wiki/AppleTalk "AppleTalk")

In November 2002, the final release of Select 2 was shipped[[41]](#cite_note-select.riscos.com-41) that included;[[42]](#cite_note-select.riscos.com2002-42)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > History of RISC OS

title: History of RISC OS
text:
- Support for [CMYK](/wiki/CMYK "CMYK") sprites
- Hardware support for the scroll wheel on [PS/2](/wiki/PS/2_connector "PS/2 connector") mice
- Support for the window manager tools to be in a configurable order
- RiscStation hardware support is now in the kernel

In June 2004 the final release of Select 3 was shipped[[41]](#cite_note-select.riscos.com-41) that included:[[43]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comS3-43)

- Cut and Paste supported in writeable icons (textboxes)
- The filer can display image thumbnails
- Button and other icons can now support rounded borders
- The sprite format now supported an [alpha channel](/wiki/Alpha_channel "Alpha channel")
- A recycle bin
- An improved version of !Paint, the bitmap editor, to support the alpha channel sprites

Also in June 2004, RISCOS Ltd released the ROM based version 4.39,[[44]](#cite_note-riscos.comRO439-44) being dubbed *RISC OS Adjust*. (The name was a play on the RISC OS GUI convention of calling the three mouse buttons 'Select', 'Menu' and 'Adjust'.) RISCOS Ltd sold its 500th Adjust ROM in early 2006.[[45]](#cite_note-riscos.com2006-45) Features introduced in 4.39 include user customization of the graphical user interface.[[46]](#cite_note-Ryan2011-46)

Further release under the Select scheme were made under the RISC OS Six branding, mentioned below.

### The A9Home

Main article: [A9home](/wiki/A9home "A9home")

The A9home, released in 2006, uses RISC OS version 4.42 *Adjust 32*. This was developed by RISCOS Ltd and supports 32-bit addressing modes found on later ARM architectures.

title: History of RISC OS
text:
### RISC OS Six

In October 2006, shortly after Castle Technology announced the Shared Source Initiative, RISCOS Ltd announced RISC OS Six, the next generation of their stream of the operating system.[[47]](#cite_note-newsfromriscos-47)

The first product to be launched under the RISC OS Six name, was the continuation of the Select scheme, Select 4.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A beta-version of RISC OS 6, Preview 1 (Select 4i1), was available in 2007 as a free download[[48]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comRO6-48) to all subscribers to the Select scheme, both present subscribers and those whose subscription was renewed after 30 May 2004 but has since lapsed.

title: History of RISC OS
text:
The first product to be launched under the RISC OS Six name, was the continuation of the Select scheme, Select 4.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A beta-version of RISC OS 6, Preview 1 (Select 4i1), was available in 2007 as a free download[[48]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comRO6-48) to all subscribers to the Select scheme, both present subscribers and those whose subscription was renewed after 30 May 2004 but has since lapsed.

RISC OS Six brought portability, stability and internal structure improvements, including full 26/32-bit neutrality. It is now highly modularised, with legacy and hardware specific features abstracted, and other code separated for easier future maintenance and development.[[49]](#cite_note-select4changes-49) Teletext support, device interrupt handler, software-based graphics operations, the real-time clock, the mouse pointer, CMOS RAM support, and hardware timer support have been abstracted out of the kernel and into their own separate modules.[[49]](#cite_note-select4changes-49) Legacy components, like the VIDC driver, and obsolete functionality for the [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro") have been abstracted too.[[49]](#cite_note-select4changes-49) AIF and transient utility executable checking has been introduced also to protect against rogue software, while graphics acceleration modules may be provided for the SM501 graphics chip in the A9home and for [ViewFinder AGP podule cards](/wiki/Risc_PC#Podule "Risc PC").[[50]](#cite_note-ROL_RO6_new_features-50) In April 2008 the final release of Select 4 was shipped that included:[[51]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comRO64i4-51)

- 8 MB VRAM support in VirtualRPC
- Filer updates, Keyboard shortcuts, alternative layouts, configurability
- [SVG](/wiki/Scalable_Vector_Graphics "Scalable Vector Graphics") export in !Draw

Select 4 releases are initially compatible with only Acorn [Risc PC](/wiki/Risc_PC "Risc PC") and [A7000](/wiki/Acorn_A7000 "Acorn A7000") machines.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] RiscStation R7500, MicroDigital Omega and Mico computers will not officially be supported, as the company does not have test machines available and requires proprietary software code to which they do not have the rights.[[52]](#cite_note-ROL_RO6_FAQ-52) Lack of detailed technical information about the MicroDigital Omega has also been cited as being another reason why support of that hardware is difficult.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In April 2009 the final release of Select 5 was shipped[[47]](#cite_note-newsfromriscos-47) that included:[[53]](#cite_note-select.riscos.comRO65i1-53)

- 64K colour screen modes
- More responsive desktop
- Improvements to !Paint and !Draw

The final release of RISC OS from RISCOS Ltd was Select 6i1, shipped in December 2009, it includes;[[54]](#cite_note-myriscos.co.ukRO62-54)

title: History of RISC OS
text:
### RISC OS 5

*RISC OS 5* is a separate evolution by [Castle Technology Ltd](/wiki/Castle_Technology_Ltd "Castle Technology Ltd") based upon work done by Pace for their NCOS based set top boxes. RISC OS 5 was written to support Castle's [Iyonix PC](/wiki/Iyonix_PC "Iyonix PC") Acorn-compatible, which runs on the [Intel XScale](/wiki/Intel_XScale "Intel XScale") ARM processor. Although a wealth of software has now been updated, a few older applications can only be run on RISC OS 5 via an emulator called Aemulor, since the [ARMv5](/wiki/ARM_core "ARM core") XScale processor does not support [26-bit](/wiki/26-bit "26-bit") addressing modes. Likewise, RISC OS 5 itself had to be ported to run properly on the new CPU, and abstraction of the graphics and other hardware interfaces created, to allow it, for example, to use standard graphics cards, instead of Acorn's own VIDC chip.

In July 2003, Castle Technology Ltd bought the head licence for RISC OS from Pace Micro.[[55]](#cite_note-drobe.co.ukBuys-55)[[56]](#cite_note-Pace_2003-07-04-56)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > History of RISC OS

title: History of RISC OS
text:
### Shared Source Initiative

In October 2006, [Castle Technology Ltd](/wiki/Castle_Technology_Ltd "Castle Technology Ltd") announced a plan to release elements of RISC OS 5 under a source sharing license. The Shared Source Initiative (SSI) was a joint venture between Castle and [RISC OS Open Limited](/wiki/RISC_OS_Open_Limited "RISC OS Open Limited") (ROOL), a newly formed software development company, which aimed to accelerate development and encourage uptake of the OS. Under the custom dual license, released source was freely available and could be modified and redistributed without royalty for non-commercial use, while commercial usage incurred a per-unit license fee to Castle.

The SSI made phased releases of source code, starting in May 2007.[[57]](#cite_note-drobe.co.ukShared-57) By October 2008, enough source was released to build an almost complete Iyonix ROM image.[[58]](#cite_note-riscosopen.org2008-58) By late 2011, it was possible to build complete ROM images from the published sources; with the full source code available as [tarballs](/wiki/Tar_(computing) "Tar (computing)"), [CVS](/wiki/Concurrent_Versions_System "Concurrent Versions System"), or a web interface to the CVS archive.

In October 2018, the rights to RISC OS 5 were acquired by RISC OS Developments, and re-licensed under the [Apache 2.0](/wiki/Apache_2.0 "Apache 2.0") license.[[59]](#cite_note-theregisterROopensource-59) ROOL continues to maintain the source tree and co-ordinates an international developer community on a non-profit basis to support and encourage development.

title: History of RISC OS
text:
In October 2018, the rights to RISC OS 5 were acquired by RISC OS Developments, and re-licensed under the [Apache 2.0](/wiki/Apache_2.0 "Apache 2.0") license.[[59]](#cite_note-theregisterROopensource-59) ROOL continues to maintain the source tree and co-ordinates an international developer community on a non-profit basis to support and encourage development.

Prebuilt images are available, as both stable releases and development "[nightly builds](/wiki/Nightly_build "Nightly build")".[[60]](#cite_note-ROM_image_releases-60)

Ports of RISC OS 5 are available for the [A7000/A7000+](/wiki/Acorn_A7000 "Acorn A7000"), [RiscPC](/wiki/RiscPC "RiscPC"), [RPCemu](/w/index.php?title=RPCemu&action=edit&redlink=1 "RPCemu (page does not exist)"), the [OMAP3](/wiki/OMAP#OMAP_3 "OMAP") [BeagleBoard](/wiki/BeagleBoard "BeagleBoard") and [derivatives](/wiki/Pandora_(console) "Pandora (console)"), [OMAP4](/wiki/OMAP#OMAP_4 "OMAP") [PandaBoard](/wiki/PandaBoard "PandaBoard") and PandaBoard ES, [OMAP5](/wiki/OMAP#OMAP_5 "OMAP") IGEPv5 and UEVM5432, [AM5728](/wiki/Sitara_ARM_Processor "Sitara ARM Processor") Titanium, the [Raspberry Pi](/wiki/Raspberry_Pi "Raspberry Pi"), and the XScale Iyonix.[[60]](#cite_note-ROM_image_releases-60)

title: Internet OS
text:
Not to be confused with [Web desktop](/wiki/Web_desktop "Web desktop").

An **Internet operating system**, or **Internet OS**, is any type of [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") designed to run all of its applications and services through an [Internet](/wiki/Internet "Internet") client,[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] generally a [web browser](/wiki/Web_browser "Web browser"). The advantages of such an OS would be that it would run on a *[thin client](/wiki/Thin_client "Thin client")*, allowing cheaper, more easily manageable computer systems; it would require all applications to be designed on [cross-platform](/wiki/Cross-platform "Cross-platform"), [open standards](/wiki/Open_standards "Open standards"); and would not tie a user's applications, documents, and preferences to a single computer, but rather place them in the [Internet cloud](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing"). The Internet OS has also been promoted as the perfect type of platform for [software as a service](/wiki/Software_as_a_service "Software as a service").
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Internet OS

title: Internet OS
text:
## History

Talk of an Internet OS began to surface in 1995 as the [browser war](/wiki/Browser_wars "Browser wars") started heating up between [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") and [Netscape](/wiki/Netscape "Netscape").

In response to the limited capabilities of [HTML](/wiki/HTML "HTML") at the time, Microsoft began developing an online content authoring platform that would be based on distributed [OLE](/wiki/Object_Linking_and_Embedding "Object Linking and Embedding") (Object Linking and Embedding) which it codenamed [Blackbird](/wiki/Blackbird_(online_platform) "Blackbird (online platform)"). Using OLE, applications put on the web would contain their own processing logic, so would act similar to applications in a typical [desktop environment](/wiki/Desktop_environment "Desktop environment").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Immediately, there were concerns that this would tie the web to [proprietary](/wiki/Proprietary_software "Proprietary software") Microsoft technology that wouldn't be guaranteed to run across different systems.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

As a challenge, [Marc Andreessen](/wiki/Marc_Andreessen "Marc Andreessen") of Netscape announced a set of new products that would help transform their browser into what he called an "Internet OS" that would provide the tools and programming interfaces for a new generation of Internet-based applications. The so-called "Internet OS" would still run on top of a regular OS – being based around Netscape Navigator – but he dismissed desktop operating systems like Windows as simply "bag[s] of drivers",[[3]](#cite_note-3) reiterating that the goal would be to "turn Windows into a mundane collection of not entirely debugged device drivers".[[4]](#cite_note-4)

text:
As a challenge, [Marc Andreessen](/wiki/Marc_Andreessen "Marc Andreessen") of Netscape announced a set of new products that would help transform their browser into what he called an "Internet OS" that would provide the tools and programming interfaces for a new generation of Internet-based applications. The so-called "Internet OS" would still run on top of a regular OS – being based around Netscape Navigator – but he dismissed desktop operating systems like Windows as simply "bag[s] of drivers",[[3]](#cite_note-3) reiterating that the goal would be to "turn Windows into a mundane collection of not entirely debugged device drivers".[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Andreessen explained that the newest versions of Navigator were not just web browsers, but suites of Internet applications, including programs for mail, FTP, news, and more, and would come with viewers for a variety of document types, like [Adobe Acrobat](/wiki/Adobe_Acrobat "Adobe Acrobat"), [Apple QuickTime](/wiki/Apple_QuickTime "Apple QuickTime"), and [Sun Java](/wiki/Sun_Java "Sun Java") applets, which would give it programming interfaces and publishing tools for developers. Netscape also would continue to sell its server software, and [Java applets](/wiki/Java_applets "Java applets") would run cross-platform on both its clients and its servers, and as a scripting language in the form of [JavaScript](/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript"). They would also provide facilities for backend transaction processing, elaborating the client/server model with navigating clients and application servers and database servers.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He pointed out – because of the broad capabilities that all of this gave their browser – the only difference technically between Netscape Navigator and a traditional operating system is that Navigator didn't include device drivers.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

text:
### The "Gang of Five" and the NC

Main article: [Network Computer](/wiki/Network_Computer "Network Computer")

Opposition in the industry to Microsoft began to grow, as did the concept of an "Internet OS", and this led to the formation of an alliance around developing Java as an alternative to Windows – the chief partners being Netscape, [Sun](/wiki/Sun_Microsystems "Sun Microsystems"), [Oracle](/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation"), and [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"). These companies were informally referred to in the industry press as the "Gang of Four". [Novell](/wiki/Novell "Novell") later joined the alliance, leading it to be called the "Gang of Five".[[8]](#cite_note-8)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Internet OS

title: Internet OS
section: The "Gang of Five" and the NC
heading_path: The "Gang of Five" and the NC
text:
Opposition in the industry to Microsoft began to grow, as did the concept of an "Internet OS", and this led to the formation of an alliance around developing Java as an alternative to Windows – the chief partners being Netscape, [Sun](/wiki/Sun_Microsystems "Sun Microsystems"), [Oracle](/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation"), and [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"). These companies were informally referred to in the industry press as the "Gang of Four". [Novell](/wiki/Novell "Novell") later joined the alliance, leading it to be called the "Gang of Five".[[8]](#cite_note-8)

In May 1997, the group published a position paper which discussed integration of software component models within [CORBA](/wiki/CORBA "CORBA") – a commonly used architecture allowing computer applications from different vendors running on different systems to work together over networks. From this, they then issued several RFPs (Request for Proposals) to the [Object Management Group](/wiki/Object_Management_Group "Object Management Group") (OMG), the standards body responsible for managing CORBA, meant to help integrate different aspects of Java. The proposals included support for [JavaBeans](/wiki/JavaBeans "JavaBeans") – the serialized, component architecture of Java – and for [JavaScript](/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript").[[9]](#cite_note-9) In what was called the "Java-tization of CORBA", the group was positioning Java to be a distributed object architecture, similar to what Microsoft had intended with OLE in Blackbird. OLE would only exist as a second-class technology that would interface through CORBA using JavaBeans.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The proposals included support for [JavaBeans](/wiki/JavaBeans "JavaBeans") – the serialized, component architecture of Java – and for [JavaScript](/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript").[[9]](#cite_note-9) In what was called the "Java-tization of CORBA", the group was positioning Java to be a distributed object architecture, similar to what Microsoft had intended with OLE in Blackbird. OLE would only exist as a second-class technology that would interface through CORBA using JavaBeans.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

The group also promoted the idea of a [JavaOS](/wiki/JavaOS "JavaOS") – a minimal, Java-based operating system – which would in turn run Netscape's web browser, and through the browser run JavaBeans components. This would be the front for a new ecosystem based on open standards; first, [HTML](/wiki/HTML "HTML") in the web browser; and second, [Java](/wiki/Java_(programming_language) "Java (programming language)"), which they hoped would become widely adopted through CORBA. JavaOS would be hosted on a Network Computer (or NC), a concept long advocated by Oracle. The NC would be a [thin client](/wiki/Thin_client "Thin client") designed only for Internet use, leaving it to access applications and documents stored entirely online. Oracle saw its role as providing tools for the server layer, where network-hosted applications would be provided through the Network Application Server, which in turn would make use of both Oracle7 relationship database management system and the Oracle Web Server. Oracle also outlined what was referred to as the [Network Computing Architecture](/w/index.php?title=Network_Computing_Architecture_(Oracle)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Network Computing Architecture (Oracle) (page does not exist)") (NCA), which would separate presentation, application and data access logic into Java applets or NCA cartridges.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Microsoft and Intel in response to this challenge put forward a standard for a competing model called the [NetPC](/wiki/NetPC "NetPC"), a diskless PC that would be primarily adapted to web browser use and would run a simplified version of [Windows 95](/wiki/Windows_95 "Windows 95"), codenamed Pegasus. Later down the road, this idea evolved into the [Netbook](/wiki/Netbook "Netbook"). Microsoft publicly criticized the idea of an Internet OS, and instead argued that the traditional desktop OS should be Internet-enabled, the beginning of the idea for [Active Platform](/wiki/Active_Platform "Active Platform"), an Internet strategy that culminated later in the release of [Windows 98](/wiki/Windows_98 "Windows 98"). This strategy, which involved tightly bundling [Internet Explorer](/wiki/Internet_Explorer "Internet Explorer") in Windows, became the center of a United States [antitrust suit](/wiki/United_States_v._Microsoft "United States v. Microsoft") against Microsoft. All of the Gang of Five – Netscape, Sun, IBM, Oracle, and Novell – were involved in lobbying for antitrust action against Microsoft.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

By 1998, the Java alliance started to fall apart. Oracle continued developing server-side Java databases but had given up the idea of the network computer and Netscape had given up on their Java browser efforts, instead aiming to position themselves as an Internet portal. Pressure from investors was given the blame.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

text:
### ChromeOS and ChromiumOS

Main articles: [ChromeOS](/wiki/ChromeOS "ChromeOS") and [ChromiumOS](/wiki/ChromiumOS "ChromiumOS")

[Google](/wiki/Google "Google") revived the idea of the Internet OS in 2009 with the development of [ChromeOS](/wiki/ChromeOS "ChromeOS"), a [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux")-based operating system designed to work exclusively with [AJAX](/wiki/AJAX "AJAX")-based web applications. The operating system was designed to look and operate like the [Chrome web browser](/wiki/Google_Chrome "Google Chrome") and be sold on laptops developed with partners, called [Chromebooks](/wiki/Chromebook "Chromebook"). They also promoted [G Suite](/wiki/G_Suite "G Suite"), their suite of web applications, as an alternative to traditional desktop software such as [Microsoft Office](/wiki/Microsoft_Office "Microsoft Office").

Google has tried to address standard criticisms of the Internet OS concept with its development projects. [Google Native Client](/wiki/Google_Native_Client "Google Native Client") allows a browser to run [Intel x86](/wiki/Intel_x86 "Intel x86") native code in a [sandbox](/wiki/Sandbox_(computer_security) "Sandbox (computer security)"), so that more complex programs could run that more fully take advantage of a system's hardware. [Google Gears](/wiki/Google_Gears "Google Gears") was also created to allow offline access of online applications, although this is being deprecated in favour of [web storage](/wiki/Web_storage "Web storage"), a model in the process of standardization by the [World Wide Web Consortium](/wiki/World_Wide_Web_Consortium "World Wide Web Consortium") (W3C).

ChromiumOS is the development version of ChromeOS, but before ChromeOS was available, ChromiumOS's principal user interface was the [Chromium](/wiki/Chromium_(web_browser) "Chromium (web browser)") web browser, which is fully free and open-source, rather than the commercial Google Chrome web browser. As such ChromiumOS does not ship with any of Google's branding and proprietary cloud services preinstalled.

title: Bare machine
text:
Computer without an operating system

"Bare metal" redirects here. For other uses, see [Bare metal (disambiguation)](/wiki/Bare_metal_(disambiguation) "Bare metal (disambiguation)").

Not to be confused with [Bare-metal server](/wiki/Bare-metal_server "Bare-metal server").

In [information technology](/wiki/Information_technology "Information technology"), a **bare machine** (or **bare-metal computer**) is a [computer](/wiki/Computer "Computer") which has no [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system").[[1]](#cite_note-databank-1) The software executed by a bare machine, a [standalone program](/wiki/Standalone_program "Standalone program") commonly called a *bare metal program* or *bare metal application*,[[2]](#cite_note-2) is designed to interact directly with hardware. Bare machines are widely used in [embedded systems](/wiki/Embedded_system "Embedded system"), particularly in cases where resources are limited or high performance is required.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Bare machine

title: Bare machine
text:
## Bare machine computing

**Bare Machine Computing** is a computing paradigm in which application software runs directly on a bare machine as a single, stand-alone executable, without an operating system or device drivers. The application software has direct access to hardware resources, and there is typically no distinction between user and kernel mode. It is self-managed software that boots, loads and runs without using any other software components. Bare metal programs are typically written in a close-to-hardware language such as [C](/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)") or [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language").[[4]](#cite_note-4)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Bare machine

title: Bare machine
text:
## Advantages

Typically, a bare-metal application will run faster, use less memory and be more power efficient than an equivalent program that relies on an operating system, due to the inherent overhead imposed by [system calls](/wiki/System_call "System call"). For example, hardware inputs and outputs are directly accessible to bare metal software, whereas they must usually be accessed through system calls when using an OS.[[5]](#cite_note-5) It has no OS and therefore has no OS-related vulnerabilities.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Bare machine

title: Bare machine
text:
## Disadvantages

Bare metal applications typically require more effort to develop because operating system services such as memory management and task scheduling are not available.

Debugging a bare-metal program may be complicated by factors such as:

- Lack of a standard output.
- The target machine may differ from the hardware used for program development (e.g., [emulator](/wiki/Emulator "Emulator"), simulator). This forces setting up a way to load the bare-metal program onto the target ([flashing](/wiki/Firmware#Flashing "Firmware")), start the program execution and access the target resources.

title: Bare machine

### Early computers

Early computers, such as the [PDP-11](/wiki/PDP-11 "PDP-11"), allowed programmers to load a program, supplied in [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code"), to [RAM](/wiki/RAM "RAM"). The resulting operation of the program could be monitored by [lights](/wiki/Blinkenlights "Blinkenlights"), and output derived from [magnetic tape](/wiki/Magnetic_tape "Magnetic tape"), print devices, or [storage](/wiki/Computer_data_storage "Computer data storage").

title: Bare machine
text:
### Embedded systems

[![Wikibooks logo](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Wikibooks-logo.svg/40px-Wikibooks-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Wikibooks-logo.svg)

The Wikibook *[Embedded Systems](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Embedded_Systems "wikibooks:Embedded Systems")* has a page on the topic of: ***[Super Loop Architecture](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Embedded_Systems/Super_Loop_Architecture "wikibooks:Embedded Systems/Super Loop Architecture")***

Bare machine programming is a common practice in [embedded systems](/wiki/Embedded_system "Embedded system"), in which [microcontrollers](/wiki/Microcontroller "Microcontroller") or [microprocessors](/wiki/Microprocessor "Microprocessor") boot directly into monolithic, single-purpose software without loading an operating system. Such [embedded software](/wiki/Embedded_software "Embedded software") can vary in structure. For example, one such program paradigm, known as *foreground-background* or **superloop** architecture, consists of an infinite [main loop](/wiki/Main_loop "Main loop") in which each task is executed sequentially and must [voluntarily return control back to the loop](/wiki/Cooperative_multitasking "Cooperative multitasking").[[6]](#cite_note-6) The loop runs these cooperative *background* processes that are not time-critical, while [interrupt service routines](/wiki/Interrupt_service_routine "Interrupt service routine") momentarily interrupt the loop to handle time-critical foreground tasks.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## A

- **[access token](/wiki/Access_token "Access token")**: In [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") [operating systems](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system"), an **access token** contains the security credentials for a [login session](/wiki/Login_session "Login session") and identifies the [user](/wiki/User_(computing) "User (computing)"), the user's groups, the user's privileges, and, in some cases, a particular application.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Glossary of operating systems terms

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## B

- **binary semaphore**: See *semaphore*.
- **[booting](/wiki/Booting "Booting")**: In [computing](/wiki/Computing "Computing"), **booting** (also known as **booting up**) is the initial set of operations that a [computer](/wiki/Computer "Computer") performs after electrical power is switched on or when the computer is reset. This can take tens of seconds and typically involves performing a [power-on self-test](/wiki/Power-on_self-test "Power-on self-test"), locating and initializing peripheral devices, and then finding, loading and starting the [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system").
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Glossary of operating systems terms

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## C

- **[cache](/wiki/Cache_(computing) "Cache (computing)")**: In [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), a **cache** is a component that transparently stores data so that future requests for that data can be served faster. The data that is stored within a cache might be values that have been computed earlier or duplicates of original values that are stored elsewhere.
- **[cloud](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing")**: Cloud computing operating systems are recent, and were not mentioned in Gagne's 8th Edition (2009).[[3]](#cite_note-Operating_Sytems_Concepts-3) In contrast, by Gagne's 9th (2012), cloud o/s received 3 pages of coverage (41, 42, 716). Doeppner (2011) mentions them (p. 3), but only to prove that operating systems "are not a solved problem" and that even if the day of the dedicated PC is waning, cloud computing has created an entirely new opportunity for o/s development ala sharing, networks, memory, parallelism, etc. Gagne (2012) adds that in addition to numerous traditional o/s's at cloud warehouses, [Virtual machine](/wiki/Virtual_machine "Virtual machine") o/s (VMMs), [Eucalyptus](/wiki/Eucalyptus_(software) "Eucalyptus (software)"), Vware, [vCloud](/wiki/VCloud "VCloud") Director and others are being developed specifically for cloud management with numerous traditional o/s features (security, threads, file and memory management, guis, etc.) (p. 42). Microsoft's investment in cloud aspects of o/s tend to support that argument.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)
- **[concurrency](/wiki/Concurrency_(computer_science) "Concurrency (computer science)")**
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Glossary of operating systems terms

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## D

- **[daemon](/wiki/Daemon_(computing) "Daemon (computing)")**: Operating systems often start daemons at [boot](/wiki/Booting "Booting") time and serve the function of responding to network requests, hardware activity, or other programs by performing some task. Daemons can also configure hardware (like [udevd](/wiki/Udev "Udev") on some [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") systems), run scheduled tasks (like [cron](/wiki/Cron "Cron")), and perform a variety of other tasks.

text:
## K

- **[kernel](/wiki/Kernel_(operating_system) "Kernel (operating system)")**: In [computing](/wiki/Computing "Computing"), the **kernel** is a [computer program](/wiki/Computer_program "Computer program") that manages [input/output](/wiki/Input/output "Input/output") requests from [software](/wiki/Software "Software") and translates them into [data processing](/wiki/Data_processing "Data processing") instructions for the [central processing unit](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and other [electronic components](/wiki/Electronic_component "Electronic component") of a [computer](/wiki/Computer "Computer"). The kernel is a fundamental part of a modern computer's [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system").
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Glossary of operating systems terms

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## L

- **[lock](/wiki/Lock_(computer_science) "Lock (computer science)")**: In [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), a **lock** or **mutex** (from [mutual exclusion](/wiki/Mutual_exclusion "Mutual exclusion")) is a [synchronization](/wiki/Synchronization_(computer_science) "Synchronization (computer science)") mechanism for enforcing limits on access to a resource in an environment where there are many [threads of execution](/wiki/Thread_(computer_science) "Thread (computer science)"). A lock is designed to enforce a [mutual exclusion](/wiki/Mutual_exclusion "Mutual exclusion") [concurrency control](/wiki/Concurrency_control "Concurrency control") policy.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Glossary of operating systems terms

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## M

- **[mutual exclusion](/wiki/Mutual_exclusion "Mutual exclusion")**: Mutual exclusion is to allow only one process at a time to access the same critical section (a part of code which accesses the critical resource). This helps prevent [race conditions](/wiki/Race_condition "Race condition").
- **mutex**: See *lock*.
