text:
## S

- **[semaphore](/wiki/Semaphore_(programming) "Semaphore (programming)")**: In computer science, particularly in operating systems, a **semaphore** is a [variable](/wiki/Variable_(computer_science) "Variable (computer science)") or [abstract data type](/wiki/Abstract_data_type "Abstract data type") that is used for controlling access, by multiple [processes](/wiki/Process_(computing) "Process (computing)"), to a common resource in a [parallel programming](/wiki/Parallel_computing "Parallel computing") or a [multi user](/wiki/Multi-user_software "Multi-user software") environment.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Glossary of operating systems terms

title: Glossary of operating systems terms
text:
## T

- **[thread](/wiki/Thread_(computing) "Thread (computing)")**: In [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), a **thread** of execution is the smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be managed independently by an [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") [scheduler](/wiki/Scheduling_(computing) "Scheduling (computing)"). The scheduler itself is a [light-weight process](/wiki/Light-weight_process "Light-weight process"). The implementation of threads and [processes](/wiki/Process_(computing) "Process (computing)") differs from one [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") to another, but in most cases, a thread is contained inside a process.
- **templating**: In an o/s context, templating refers to creating a single virtual machine image as a guest operating system, then saving it as a tool for multiple running virtual machines (Gagne, 2012, p. 716). The technique is used both in virtualization and cloud computing management, and is common in large server warehouses.

The **Holborn 9100** was a personal computer introduced in 1981 by a small [Dutch](/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") company called [Holborn](/w/index.php?title=Holborn_(company)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Holborn (company) (page does not exist)") [[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holborn_(bedrijf) "nl:Holborn (bedrijf)")]. Only around 200 of these devices were sold, with Holborn going into [bankruptcy](/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy") in 1983.

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## History

The Holborn 9100 was released in 1981 by Dutch computer manufacturer Holborn. The appearance was designed by an industrial design office named Studio Vos and developed by Hans Polak and Henny Beavers. The name comes from the phrase "born in Holland." There were two main versions, a larger one with a proprietary multi-user operating system named Holborn OS with support for a [light pen](/wiki/Light_pen "Light pen"), and a smaller machine with the operating system [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") and no light pen support.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

These versions were split into four different models released: the 9100, 7100, 6500, and 6100. The systems consist primarily of a combined desktop [monitor](/wiki/Computer_monitor "Computer monitor"), [terminal](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal"), and [keyboard](/wiki/Computer_keyboard "Computer keyboard") with an external unit housing two 8 inch [floppy drives](/wiki/Floppy_drives "Floppy drives") and an optional [hard drive](/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive"). The 6500 series had a detachable keyboard.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The computer was primarily marketed to small companies for administration and bookkeeping purposes.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) The lower-numbered models were produced after the release of the 9100.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Around 200 machines were produced, with 50 of them being the larger models.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)

title: Holborn 9100

These versions were split into four different models released: the 9100, 7100, 6500, and 6100. The systems consist primarily of a combined desktop [monitor](/wiki/Computer_monitor "Computer monitor"), [terminal](/wiki/Computer_terminal "Computer terminal"), and [keyboard](/wiki/Computer_keyboard "Computer keyboard") with an external unit housing two 8 inch [floppy drives](/wiki/Floppy_drives "Floppy drives") and an optional [hard drive](/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive"). The 6500 series had a detachable keyboard.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) The computer was primarily marketed to small companies for administration and bookkeeping purposes.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) The lower-numbered models were produced after the release of the 9100.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Around 200 machines were produced, with 50 of them being the larger models.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)

Due to the high price of the system at the time at 30,000 [guilder](/wiki/Dutch_guilder "Dutch guilder")[[3]](#cite_note-3) or $10,000 USD (equivalent to $30,591 in 2023) and competition from [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), the system was a commercial failure and caused the manufacturer to go bankrupt in 1983. The most popular version was the 6100.[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4) It is estimated that around 20 systems survive.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

## Specifications

- OS: Holborn OS or [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M")
- CPU: [Zilog Z80A](/wiki/Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80") at 4 MHz

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## Holborn OS

Holborn OS (HOS) was a multi-user [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") developed by Holborn. It was stored entirely on [ROM](/wiki/ROM "ROM") and used floppy disks to start applications.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5) The application software was menu driven and could be controlled by a light pen to aid use by technically unskilled users.[[6]](#cite_note-:4-6)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Holborn 9100

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## Holborn

Holborn Computers was founded in 1979 by Hans Polak and Dick Gerdzen. The goal of the company was to supply computers based on [microprocessor](/wiki/Microprocessor "Microprocessor") technology to specific types of retailers.[[6]](#cite_note-:4-6) The company saw a market for cheaper computer systems as IBM computers were expensive at the time. Henny Beavers joined soon afterwards. The company aimed to design and manufacture the systems as quickly as possible to get them out in the market.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5)

Once the Holborn 9100 was released in 1981, they marketed it using displays at [trade shows](/wiki/Trade_show "Trade show") and advertisements. Due to competition from more popular IBM computers, Holborn remained dependent on financial aid from the [Overijssel](/wiki/Overijssel "Overijssel") development company OOM.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5) OOM could not supply enough financial resources and Gerdzen had to leave the company, causing the company to go bankrupt on 27 April 1983. They ultimately considered the 9100 a failure.[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4)
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > Holborn 9100

title: Holborn 9100
text:
## Reception

The Holborn 9100 is noted for its design, being referred to as "something out of a [retro-futuristic](/wiki/Retrofuturism "Retrofuturism") movie" by cybernews.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Inexhibit noted that "The design of the Holborn set it apart from most computers of the time," calling it futuristic and organic.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

Computer [operating systems](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") (OSes) provide a set of functions needed and used by most application programs on a computer, and the links needed to control and synchronize computer hardware. On the first computers, with no operating system, every program needed the full hardware specification to run correctly and perform standard tasks, and its own drivers for [peripheral](/wiki/Peripheral "Peripheral") devices like printers and [punched paper card readers](/wiki/Punched_card "Punched card"). The growing complexity of hardware and application programs eventually made operating systems a necessity for everyday use.

title: History of operating systems
text:
Early computers lacked any form of operating system. Instead, the user (rarely also the computer operator), had sole use of the machine for a scheduled period of time. The user would deliver his program to a computer operator who would be responsible for loading the computer with the program and data needed for its 'run'.

Eventually, the end of a user's program could be detected and a control program automatically loaded which would load the next user's program, relieving the operator of having to load in each user's program individually and introducing the era of 'batched' programming. That is, a number of user programs could all be loaded together in a batch. Loading of program and data was accomplished in various ways including toggle switches (only used by a user on the earliest of computers, but later used by the computer operator to control the computer, e.g., to start it up, to shut it down, to 'pause', to 'dump' its RAM contents, and/or to control its input and/or its output), punched paper cards and magnetic or paper tape.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Once loaded, the machine would be set to execute each program singly until that program completed, crashed, exceeded its time limit or went into a(n infinite) loop. In those early days, there were only 'Control Program' units for providing the software necessary to control the computers and ancillary hardware, e.g., for such semi hardware functions as I/O . None of the early 'Control Programs' were sufficiently sophisticated to recognize a looping user program or initiate a recovery action.

title: History of operating systems
text:
Eventually, the end of a user's program could be detected and a control program automatically loaded which would load the next user's program, relieving the operator of having to load in each user's program individually and introducing the era of 'batched' programming. That is, a number of user programs could all be loaded together in a batch. Loading of program and data was accomplished in various ways including toggle switches (only used by a user on the earliest of computers, but later used by the computer operator to control the computer, e.g., to start it up, to shut it down, to 'pause', to 'dump' its RAM contents, and/or to control its input and/or its output), punched paper cards and magnetic or paper tape.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Once loaded, the machine would be set to execute each program singly until that program completed, crashed, exceeded its time limit or went into a(n infinite) loop. In those early days, there were only 'Control Program' units for providing the software necessary to control the computers and ancillary hardware, e.g., for such semi hardware functions as I/O . None of the early 'Control Programs' were sufficiently sophisticated to recognize a looping user program or initiate a recovery action.

Detection and recovery from a looping program was another critical operator function and was usually detected by the sound of the looping computer, whereupon the operator would simply initiate a complete dump of the executing program (for later debugging by the programmer) and then load in (or instruct the computer to go on to) the next user's program. Programs could sometimes be debugged via a control panel using dials, toggle switches and panel lights, making it a very manual and error-prone process.[[4]](#cite_note-4) But, this was quite rare, since the high cost of even the simplest of the early computers prohibited such exclusive use of a computer by an individual programmer. Almost all program debugging was done away from any computer by the original programmer perusing the program and the dump of its execution obtained, e.g., by the computer operator or automatically by some computer hardware exception detection (such as a timeout, an attempt to divide by zero, or an over or underflow). Programmers then could only very rarely have more than one computer 'run' per day!

[Assemblers](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language")[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) and [compilers](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler") were developed for programmers to translate program [source code](/wiki/Source_code "Source code") written in a symbolic language into [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code") that previously would have been hand-encoded. Later machines came with libraries of support code on punched cards or magnetic tape, which would be linked to the user's program to assist in operations such as input and output. This was the genesis of the modern-day operating system; however, machines still ran a single program or job at a time. At [Cambridge University](/wiki/Cambridge_University "Cambridge University") in England the job queue was at one time a string from which tapes attached to corresponding job tickets were hung with stationery pegs.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

title: History of operating systems
text:
## Mainframes

The first operating system used for real work was [GM-NAA I/O](/wiki/GM-NAA_I/O "GM-NAA I/O"), produced in 1956 by [General Motors](/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors")' Research division[[9]](#cite_note-9) for its [IBM 704](/wiki/IBM_704 "IBM 704").[[10]](#cite_note-CHM-1956-SW-10)[*[specify](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")*] Most other early operating systems for IBM mainframes were also produced by customers.[[11]](#cite_note-bozemanlugHistoryOfLinux-11)

Early operating systems were very diverse, with each vendor or customer producing one or more operating systems specific to their particular [mainframe computer](/wiki/Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer"). Every operating system, even from the same vendor, could have radically different models of commands, operating procedures, and such facilities as debugging aids. Typically, each time the manufacturer brought out a new machine, there would be a new operating system, and most applications would have to be manually adjusted, recompiled, and retested.

title: History of operating systems
text:
### Systems on IBM hardware

Main article: [History of IBM mainframe operating systems](/wiki/History_of_IBM_mainframe_operating_systems "History of IBM mainframe operating systems")

Building on customer experience and requirements, IBM took on a more active role in developing operating systems for the [709](/wiki/IBM_709 "IBM 709"), [1410](/wiki/IBM_1410 "IBM 1410"), [7010](/wiki/IBM_7010 "IBM 7010"), [7040](/wiki/IBM_7040 "IBM 7040"), [7044](/wiki/IBM_7044 "IBM 7044"), [7090](/wiki/IBM_7090 "IBM 7090") and [7094](/wiki/IBM_7094 "IBM 7094"). IBM also collaborated with universities.

The state of affairs continued until the mid 1960s when [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), already a leading hardware vendor, stopped work on existing systems and put all its effort into developing the [System/360](/wiki/IBM_System/360 "IBM System/360") series of machines, all of which used the *same* instruction and input/output architecture. IBM intended to develop a single operating system for the new hardware, the [OS/360](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors"). The problems encountered in the development of the OS/360 are legendary, and are described by [Fred Brooks](/wiki/Fred_Brooks "Fred Brooks") in *[The Mythical Man-Month](/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month "The Mythical Man-Month")*—a book that has become a classic of [software engineering](/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering"). Because of performance differences across the hardware range and delays with software development, a whole family of operating systems was introduced instead of a single OS/360.[[12]](#cite_note-JohnsonVSEPast40Years-12)[[13]](#cite_note-Boyer360Revolution-13)

title: History of operating systems
text:
The state of affairs continued until the mid 1960s when [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"), already a leading hardware vendor, stopped work on existing systems and put all its effort into developing the [System/360](/wiki/IBM_System/360 "IBM System/360") series of machines, all of which used the *same* instruction and input/output architecture. IBM intended to develop a single operating system for the new hardware, the [OS/360](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors"). The problems encountered in the development of the OS/360 are legendary, and are described by [Fred Brooks](/wiki/Fred_Brooks "Fred Brooks") in *[The Mythical Man-Month](/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month "The Mythical Man-Month")*—a book that has become a classic of [software engineering](/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering"). Because of performance differences across the hardware range and delays with software development, a whole family of operating systems was introduced instead of a single OS/360.[[12]](#cite_note-JohnsonVSEPast40Years-12)[[13]](#cite_note-Boyer360Revolution-13)

IBM wound up releasing a series of stop-gaps followed by two longer-lived operating systems:

- [OS/360](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors") for mid-range and large systems. This was available in three [system generation](/wiki/System_Generation_(OS) "System Generation (OS)") options:
  - [PCP](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#PCP "OS/360 and successors") for early users and for those without the resources for multiprogramming.
  - [MFT](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#MFT "OS/360 and successors") for mid-range systems, replaced by MFT-II in OS/360 Release 15/16. This had one successor, [OS/VS1](/wiki/OS/VS1 "OS/VS1"), which was discontinued in the 1980s.
  - [MVT](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#MVT "OS/360 and successors") for large systems. This was similar in most ways to PCP and MFT (most programs could be ported among the three without being [re-compiled](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler")), but has more sophisticated memory management and a [time-sharing](/wiki/Time-sharing "Time-sharing") facility, [TSO](/wiki/Time_Sharing_Option "Time Sharing Option"). MVT had several successors including the current [z/OS](/wiki/Z/OS "Z/OS").
- [DOS/360](/wiki/DOS/360_and_successors "DOS/360 and successors") for small System/360 models had several successors including the current [z/VSE](/wiki/VSE_(operating_system) "VSE (operating system)"). It was significantly different from OS/360.
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > History of operating systems

- [OS/360](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors "OS/360 and successors") for mid-range and large systems. This was available in three [system generation](/wiki/System_Generation_(OS) "System Generation (OS)") options:
  - [PCP](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#PCP "OS/360 and successors") for early users and for those without the resources for multiprogramming.
  - [MFT](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#MFT "OS/360 and successors") for mid-range systems, replaced by MFT-II in OS/360 Release 15/16. This had one successor, [OS/VS1](/wiki/OS/VS1 "OS/VS1"), which was discontinued in the 1980s.
  - [MVT](/wiki/OS/360_and_successors#MVT "OS/360 and successors") for large systems. This was similar in most ways to PCP and MFT (most programs could be ported among the three without being [re-compiled](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler")), but has more sophisticated memory management and a [time-sharing](/wiki/Time-sharing "Time-sharing") facility, [TSO](/wiki/Time_Sharing_Option "Time Sharing Option"). MVT had several successors including the current [z/OS](/wiki/Z/OS "Z/OS").
- [DOS/360](/wiki/DOS/360_and_successors "DOS/360 and successors") for small System/360 models had several successors including the current [z/VSE](/wiki/VSE_(operating_system) "VSE (operating system)"). It was significantly different from OS/360.

IBM maintained full compatibility with the past, so that programs developed in the sixties can still run under z/VSE (if developed for DOS/360) or z/OS (if developed for MFT or MVT) with no change.

IBM maintained full compatibility with the past, so that programs developed in the sixties can still run under z/VSE (if developed for DOS/360) or z/OS (if developed for MFT or MVT) with no change.

IBM also developed [TSS/360](/wiki/TSS_(operating_system) "TSS (operating system)"), a time-sharing system for the [System/360 Model 67](/wiki/IBM_System/360_Model_67 "IBM System/360 Model 67"). Overcompensating for their perceived importance of developing a timeshare system, they set hundreds of developers to work on the project. Early releases of TSS were slow and unreliable; by the time TSS had acceptable performance and reliability, IBM wanted its TSS users to migrate to OS/360 and OS/VS2; while IBM offered a TSS/370 PRPQ, they dropped it after 3 releases.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Several operating systems for the IBM S/360 and S/370 architectures were developed by third parties, including the [Michigan Terminal System](/wiki/Michigan_Terminal_System "Michigan Terminal System") (MTS) and [MUSIC/SP](/wiki/MUSIC/SP "MUSIC/SP").

title: History of operating systems
text:
### Other mainframe operating systems

[Control Data Corporation](/wiki/Control_Data_Corporation "Control Data Corporation") developed the [SCOPE](/wiki/CDC_SCOPE "CDC SCOPE") operating systems[[NB 1]](#cite_note-15) in the 1960s, for [batch processing](/wiki/Batch_processing "Batch processing") and later developed the [MACE](/wiki/CDC_Kronos "CDC Kronos") operating system for time sharing, which was the basis for the later [Kronos](/wiki/CDC_Kronos "CDC Kronos"). In cooperation with the [University of Minnesota](/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota"), the Kronos and later the [NOS](/wiki/NOS_(operating_system) "NOS (operating system)") operating systems were developed during the 1970s, which supported simultaneous batch and time sharing use. Like many commercial time sharing systems, its interface was an extension of the [DTSS](/wiki/Dartmouth_Time-Sharing_System "Dartmouth Time-Sharing System") time sharing system, one of the pioneering efforts in timesharing and programming languages.

In the late 1970s, Control Data and the [University of Illinois](/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Urbana%E2%80%93Champaign "University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign") developed the [PLATO system](/wiki/PLATO_(computer_system) "PLATO (computer system)"), which used plasma panel displays and long-distance time sharing networks. PLATO was remarkably innovative for its time; the shared memory model of PLATO's [TUTOR programming language](/wiki/TUTOR_(programming_language) "TUTOR (programming language)") allowed applications such as real-time chat and multi-user graphical games.

title: History of operating systems
text:
In the late 1970s, Control Data and the [University of Illinois](/wiki/University_of_Illinois_at_Urbana%E2%80%93Champaign "University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign") developed the [PLATO system](/wiki/PLATO_(computer_system) "PLATO (computer system)"), which used plasma panel displays and long-distance time sharing networks. PLATO was remarkably innovative for its time; the shared memory model of PLATO's [TUTOR programming language](/wiki/TUTOR_(programming_language) "TUTOR (programming language)") allowed applications such as real-time chat and multi-user graphical games.

For the [UNIVAC 1107](/wiki/UNIVAC_1100/2200_series#1107 "UNIVAC 1100/2200 series"), [UNIVAC](/wiki/UNIVAC "UNIVAC"), the first commercial computer manufacturer, produced the [EXEC I](/wiki/UNIVAC_EXEC_I "UNIVAC EXEC I") operating system, and [Computer Sciences Corporation](/wiki/Computer_Sciences_Corporation "Computer Sciences Corporation") developed the [EXEC II](/wiki/UNIVAC_EXEC_II "UNIVAC EXEC II") operating system and delivered it to UNIVAC. EXEC II was ported to the [UNIVAC 1108](/wiki/UNIVAC_1100/2200_series#1108 "UNIVAC 1100/2200 series"). Later, UNIVAC developed the [EXEC 8](/wiki/OS_2200#Exec_8 "OS 2200") operating system for the 1108; it was the basis for operating systems for later members of the family. Like all early mainframe systems, EXEC I and EXEC II were a batch-oriented system that managed magnetic drums, disks, card readers and line printers; EXEC 8 supported both batch processing and on-line transaction processing. In the 1970s, UNIVAC produced the Real-Time Basic (RTB) system to support large-scale time sharing, also patterned after the [Dartmouth BASIC](/wiki/Dartmouth_BASIC "Dartmouth BASIC") system.

Later, UNIVAC developed the [EXEC 8](/wiki/OS_2200#Exec_8 "OS 2200") operating system for the 1108; it was the basis for operating systems for later members of the family. Like all early mainframe systems, EXEC I and EXEC II were a batch-oriented system that managed magnetic drums, disks, card readers and line printers; EXEC 8 supported both batch processing and on-line transaction processing. In the 1970s, UNIVAC produced the Real-Time Basic (RTB) system to support large-scale time sharing, also patterned after the [Dartmouth BASIC](/wiki/Dartmouth_BASIC "Dartmouth BASIC") system.

[Burroughs Corporation](/wiki/Burroughs_Corporation "Burroughs Corporation") introduced the [B5000](/wiki/Burroughs_Large_Systems "Burroughs Large Systems") in 1961 with the MCP ([Master Control Program](/wiki/Burroughs_MCP "Burroughs MCP")) operating system. The B5000 was a stack machine designed to exclusively support high-level languages, with no software, not even at the lowest level of the operating system, being written directly in [machine language](/wiki/Machine_language "Machine language") or [assembly language](/wiki/Assembly_language "Assembly language"); the MCP was the first[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] OS to be written entirely in a high-level language - [ESPOL](/wiki/Executive_Systems_Problem_Oriented_Language "Executive Systems Problem Oriented Language"), a dialect of [ALGOL 60](/wiki/ALGOL_60 "ALGOL 60") - although ESPOL had specialized statements for each "syllable"[[NB 2]](#cite_note-16) in the B5000 instruction set. MCP also introduced many other ground-breaking innovations, such as being one of[[NB 3]](#cite_note-17) the first commercial implementations of [virtual memory](/wiki/Virtual_memory "Virtual memory"). The rewrite of MCP for the B6500 is now marketed as the [Unisys](/wiki/Unisys "Unisys") ClearPath/MCP.

[Project MAC](/wiki/MIT_Computer_Science_and_Artificial_Intelligence_Laboratory#Project_MAC "MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory") at MIT, working with GE and [Bell Labs](/wiki/Bell_Labs "Bell Labs"), developed [Multics](/wiki/Multics "Multics"), which introduced the concept of ringed security privilege levels.

[Digital Equipment Corporation](/wiki/Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation") developed [TOPS-10](/wiki/TOPS-10 "TOPS-10") for its [PDP-10](/wiki/PDP-10 "PDP-10") line of 36-bit computers in 1967. Before the widespread use of Unix, TOPS-10 was a particularly popular system in universities, and in the early [ARPANET](/wiki/ARPANET "ARPANET") community. [Bolt, Beranek, and Newman](/wiki/BBN_Technologies "BBN Technologies") developed [TENEX](/wiki/TENEX_(operating_system) "TENEX (operating system)") for a modified PDP-10 that supported [demand paging](/wiki/Demand_paging "Demand paging"); this was another popular system in the research and ARPANET communities, and was later developed by DEC into [TOPS-20](/wiki/TOPS-20 "TOPS-20").

[Scientific Data Systems](/wiki/Scientific_Data_Systems "Scientific Data Systems")/Xerox Data Systems developed several operating systems for the [Sigma series](/wiki/SDS_Sigma_series "SDS Sigma series") of computers, such as the Basic Control Monitor (BCM), Batch Processing Monitor (BPM), and Basic Time-Sharing Monitor (BTM). Later, BPM and BTM were succeeded by the [Universal Time-Sharing System](/wiki/Universal_Time-Sharing_System "Universal Time-Sharing System") (UTS); it was designed to provide multi-programming services for online (interactive) user programs in addition to batch-mode production jobs, It was succeeded by the [CP-V](/wiki/CP-V "CP-V") operating system, which combined UTS with the heavily batch-oriented [Xerox Operating System](/wiki/Xerox_Operating_System "Xerox Operating System").

title: History of operating systems
text:
## Minicomputers

Digital Equipment Corporation created several operating systems for its 16-bit [PDP-11](/wiki/PDP-11 "PDP-11") machines, including the simple [RT-11](/wiki/RT-11 "RT-11") system, the time-sharing [RSTS](/wiki/RSTS/E "RSTS/E") operating systems, and the [RSX-11](/wiki/RSX-11 "RSX-11") family of [real-time operating systems](/wiki/Real-time_operating_system "Real-time operating system"), as well as the [VMS](/wiki/OpenVMS "OpenVMS") system for the 32-bit [VAX](/wiki/VAX "VAX") machines.

Several competitors of Digital Equipment Corporation such as [Data General](/wiki/Data_General "Data General"), [Hewlett-Packard](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard"), and [Computer Automation](/wiki/Computer_Automation "Computer Automation") created their own operating systems. One such, "MAX III", was developed for [Modular Computer Systems](/wiki/MODCOMP "MODCOMP") Modcomp II and Modcomp III computers. It was characterised by its target market being the industrial control market. The Fortran libraries included one that enabled access to measurement and control devices.

title: History of operating systems
text:
Several competitors of Digital Equipment Corporation such as [Data General](/wiki/Data_General "Data General"), [Hewlett-Packard](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard"), and [Computer Automation](/wiki/Computer_Automation "Computer Automation") created their own operating systems. One such, "MAX III", was developed for [Modular Computer Systems](/wiki/MODCOMP "MODCOMP") Modcomp II and Modcomp III computers. It was characterised by its target market being the industrial control market. The Fortran libraries included one that enabled access to measurement and control devices.

IBM's key innovation in operating systems in this class (which they call "mid-range"), was their "CPF" for the [System/38](/wiki/IBM_System/38 "IBM System/38"). This had [capability-based addressing](/wiki/Capability-based_addressing "Capability-based addressing"), used a machine interface architecture to isolate the application software and most of the operating system from hardware dependencies (including even such details as address size and register size) and included an integrated [RDBMS](/wiki/Relational_database_management_system "Relational database management system"). The succeeding OS/400 (now known as [IBM i](/wiki/IBM_i "IBM i")) for the [IBM AS/400](/wiki/IBM_AS/400 "IBM AS/400") and later [IBM Power Systems](/wiki/IBM_Power_Systems "IBM Power Systems") has no files, only objects of different types and these objects persist in very large, flat virtual memory, called a single-level store.

title: History of operating systems
text:
IBM's key innovation in operating systems in this class (which they call "mid-range"), was their "CPF" for the [System/38](/wiki/IBM_System/38 "IBM System/38"). This had [capability-based addressing](/wiki/Capability-based_addressing "Capability-based addressing"), used a machine interface architecture to isolate the application software and most of the operating system from hardware dependencies (including even such details as address size and register size) and included an integrated [RDBMS](/wiki/Relational_database_management_system "Relational database management system"). The succeeding OS/400 (now known as [IBM i](/wiki/IBM_i "IBM i")) for the [IBM AS/400](/wiki/IBM_AS/400 "IBM AS/400") and later [IBM Power Systems](/wiki/IBM_Power_Systems "IBM Power Systems") has no files, only objects of different types and these objects persist in very large, flat virtual memory, called a single-level store.

The [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") operating system was developed at AT&T Bell Laboratories in the late 1960s, originally for the [PDP-7](/wiki/PDP-7 "PDP-7"), and later for the PDP-11. Because it was essentially free in early editions, easily obtainable, and easily modified, it achieved wide acceptance. It also became a requirement within the Bell systems operating companies. Since it was written in the [C language](/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)"), when that language was ported to a new machine architecture, Unix was also able to be ported. This portability permitted it to become the choice for a second generation of minicomputers and the first generation of [workstations](/wiki/Workstation "Workstation"), and its use became widespread. Unix exemplified the idea of an operating system that was conceptually the same across various hardware platforms. Because of its utility, it inspired many and later became one of the roots of the [free software](/wiki/Free_software "Free software") movement and [open-source software](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software"). Numerous operating systems were based upon it including [Minix](/wiki/Minix "Minix"), [Linux](/wiki/History_of_Linux "History of Linux"), and the [Berkeley Software Distribution](/wiki/Berkeley_Software_Distribution "Berkeley Software Distribution"). Apple's [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") is also based on Unix via [NeXTSTEP](/wiki/NeXTSTEP "NeXTSTEP")[[15]](#cite_note-18) and [FreeBSD](/wiki/FreeBSD "FreeBSD").[[16]](#cite_note-19)

The [Pick operating system](/wiki/Pick_operating_system "Pick operating system") was another operating system available on a wide variety of hardware brands. Commercially released in 1973 its core was a [BASIC](/wiki/BASIC "BASIC")-like language called Data/BASIC and a SQL-style database manipulation language called ENGLISH. Licensed to a large variety of manufacturers and vendors, by the early 1980s observers saw the Pick operating system as a strong competitor to Unix.[[17]](#cite_note-fiedler198310-20)

## Microcomputers

Beginning in the mid-1970s, a new class of small computers came onto the marketplace. Featuring 8-bit processors, typically the [MOS Technology 6502](/wiki/MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502"), [Intel 8080](/wiki/Intel_8080 "Intel 8080"), [Motorola 6800](/wiki/Motorola_6800 "Motorola 6800") or the [Zilog Z80](/wiki/Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80"), along with rudimentary input and output interfaces and as much [RAM](/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") as practical, these systems started out as kit-based hobbyist computers but soon evolved into an essential business tool.

title: History of operating systems
text:
### Home computers

While many eight-bit [home computers](/wiki/Home_computer "Home computer") of the 1980s, such as the [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro"), [Commodore 64](/wiki/Commodore_64 "Commodore 64"), [Apple II](/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"), [Atari 8-bit computers](/wiki/Atari_8-bit_computers "Atari 8-bit computers"), [Amstrad CPC](/wiki/Amstrad_CPC "Amstrad CPC"), [ZX Spectrum](/wiki/ZX_Spectrum "ZX Spectrum") series and others could load a third-party disk-loading operating system, such as [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") or [GEOS](/wiki/GEOS_(8-bit_operating_system) "GEOS (8-bit operating system)"), they were generally used without one. Their built-in operating systems were designed in an era when [floppy disk drives](/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk") were very expensive and not expected to be used by most users, so the standard storage device on most was a [tape drive](/wiki/Tape_drive "Tape drive") using standard [compact cassettes](/wiki/Compact_Cassette "Compact Cassette"). Most, if not all, of these computers shipped with a built-in [BASIC](/wiki/BASIC "BASIC") interpreter on ROM, which also served as a crude [command-line interface](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface"), allowing the user to load a separate [disk operating system](/wiki/Disk_operating_system "Disk operating system") to perform [file management](/wiki/File_management "File management") commands and load and save to disk.

text:
While many eight-bit [home computers](/wiki/Home_computer "Home computer") of the 1980s, such as the [BBC Micro](/wiki/BBC_Micro "BBC Micro"), [Commodore 64](/wiki/Commodore_64 "Commodore 64"), [Apple II](/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"), [Atari 8-bit computers](/wiki/Atari_8-bit_computers "Atari 8-bit computers"), [Amstrad CPC](/wiki/Amstrad_CPC "Amstrad CPC"), [ZX Spectrum](/wiki/ZX_Spectrum "ZX Spectrum") series and others could load a third-party disk-loading operating system, such as [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M") or [GEOS](/wiki/GEOS_(8-bit_operating_system) "GEOS (8-bit operating system)"), they were generally used without one. Their built-in operating systems were designed in an era when [floppy disk drives](/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk") were very expensive and not expected to be used by most users, so the standard storage device on most was a [tape drive](/wiki/Tape_drive "Tape drive") using standard [compact cassettes](/wiki/Compact_Cassette "Compact Cassette"). Most, if not all, of these computers shipped with a built-in [BASIC](/wiki/BASIC "BASIC") interpreter on ROM, which also served as a crude [command-line interface](/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface"), allowing the user to load a separate [disk operating system](/wiki/Disk_operating_system "Disk operating system") to perform [file management](/wiki/File_management "File management") commands and load and save to disk.

The most popular[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] home computer, the Commodore 64, was a notable exception, as its DOS was on ROM in the disk drive hardware, and the drive was addressed identically to printers, modems, and other external devices.

title: History of operating systems
text:
The most popular[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] home computer, the Commodore 64, was a notable exception, as its DOS was on ROM in the disk drive hardware, and the drive was addressed identically to printers, modems, and other external devices.

Furthermore, those systems shipped with minimal amounts of [computer memory](/wiki/Computer_memory "Computer memory")—4-8 [kilobytes](/wiki/Kilobyte "Kilobyte") was standard on early home computers—as well as 8-bit processors without specialized support circuitry like an [MMU](/wiki/Memory_Management_Unit "Memory Management Unit") or even a dedicated [real-time clock](/wiki/Real-time_clock "Real-time clock"). On this hardware, a complex operating system's [overhead](/wiki/Overhead_(computing) "Overhead (computing)") supporting multiple tasks and users would likely compromise the performance of the machine without really being needed. As those systems were largely sold complete, with a fixed hardware configuration, there was also no need for an operating system to provide drivers for a wide range of hardware to abstract away differences.

As those systems were largely sold complete, with a fixed hardware configuration, there was also no need for an operating system to provide drivers for a wide range of hardware to abstract away differences.

[Video games](/wiki/Video_game "Video game") and even the available [spreadsheet](/wiki/Spreadsheet "Spreadsheet"), [database](/wiki/Database "Database") and [word processors](/wiki/Word_processor "Word processor") for home computers were mostly self-contained programs that took over the machine completely. Although [integrated software](/wiki/Integrated_software "Integrated software") existed for these computers, they usually lacked features compared to their standalone equivalents, largely due to memory limitations. Data exchange was mostly performed through standard formats like [ASCII](/wiki/ASCII "ASCII") text or [CSV](/wiki/Comma-separated_values "Comma-separated values"), or through specialized file conversion programs.

Modern-day game consoles and videogames, starting with the [PC-Engine](/wiki/TurboGrafx-16 "TurboGrafx-16"), all have a minimal BIOS that also provides some interactive utilities such as [memory card](/wiki/Memory_card "Memory card") management, [audio](/wiki/Compact_Disc_Digital_Audio "Compact Disc Digital Audio") or [video CD](/wiki/Video_CD "Video CD") playback, [copy protection](/wiki/Copy_protection "Copy protection") and sometimes carry [libraries](/wiki/Libraries "Libraries") for developers to use etc. Few of these cases, however, would qualify as a true operating system.

text:
Modern-day game consoles and videogames, starting with the [PC-Engine](/wiki/TurboGrafx-16 "TurboGrafx-16"), all have a minimal BIOS that also provides some interactive utilities such as [memory card](/wiki/Memory_card "Memory card") management, [audio](/wiki/Compact_Disc_Digital_Audio "Compact Disc Digital Audio") or [video CD](/wiki/Video_CD "Video CD") playback, [copy protection](/wiki/Copy_protection "Copy protection") and sometimes carry [libraries](/wiki/Libraries "Libraries") for developers to use etc. Few of these cases, however, would qualify as a true operating system.

The most notable exceptions are probably the [Dreamcast](/wiki/Dreamcast "Dreamcast") game console which includes a minimal BIOS, like the [PlayStation](/wiki/PlayStation_(console) "PlayStation (console)"), but can load the [Windows CE](/wiki/Windows_CE "Windows CE") operating system from the game disk allowing easily porting of games from the [PC](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") world, and the [Xbox](/wiki/Xbox_(console) "Xbox (console)") game console, which is little more than a disguised Intel-based [PC](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") running a secret, modified version of [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") in the background. Furthermore, there are [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") versions that will run on a [Dreamcast](/wiki/Dreamcast "Dreamcast") and later game consoles as well.

Furthermore, there are [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") versions that will run on a [Dreamcast](/wiki/Dreamcast "Dreamcast") and later game consoles as well.

Long before that, [Sony](/wiki/Sony "Sony") had released a kind of [development kit](/wiki/Game_development_kit "Game development kit") called the [Net Yaroze](/wiki/Net_Yaroze "Net Yaroze") for its first PlayStation platform, which provided a series of programming and developing tools to be used with a normal PC and a specially modified "Black PlayStation" that could be interfaced with a PC and download programs from it. These operations require in general a functional OS on both platforms involved.

These operations require in general a functional OS on both platforms involved.

In general, it can be said that videogame consoles and arcade coin-operated machines used at most a built-in [BIOS](/wiki/BIOS "BIOS") during the 1970s, 1980s and most of the 1990s, while from the PlayStation era and beyond they started getting more and more sophisticated, to the point of requiring a generic or custom-built OS for aiding in development and expandability.

text:
### Personal computer era

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Apple_Lisa_%28Little_Apple_Museum%29_%288032162544%29.jpg/250px-Apple_Lisa_%28Little_Apple_Museum%29_%288032162544%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Apple_Lisa_(Little_Apple_Museum)_(8032162544).jpg)

title: History of operating systems
text:
[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Apple_Lisa_%28Little_Apple_Museum%29_%288032162544%29.jpg/250px-Apple_Lisa_%28Little_Apple_Museum%29_%288032162544%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Apple_Lisa_(Little_Apple_Museum)_(8032162544).jpg)

Apple Lisa running Lisa OS

The development of microprocessors made inexpensive computing available for the [small business](/wiki/Small_business "Small business") and hobbyist, which in turn led to the widespread use of interchangeable hardware components using a common interconnection (such as the [S-100](/wiki/S-100_bus "S-100 bus"), SS-50, [Apple II](/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"), [ISA](/wiki/Industry_Standard_Architecture "Industry Standard Architecture"), and [PCI](/wiki/Conventional_PCI "Conventional PCI") [buses](/wiki/Bus_(computing) "Bus (computing)")), and an increasing need for "standard" operating systems to control them. The most important of the early OSes on these machines was [Digital Research](/wiki/Digital_Research "Digital Research")'s [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M")-80 for the 8080 / 8085 / Z80 CPUs. It was based on several Digital Equipment Corporation operating systems, mostly for the PDP-11 architecture. Microsoft's first operating system, [MDOS/MIDAS](/wiki/Marc_McDonald "Marc McDonald"), was designed along many of the PDP-11 features, but for microprocessor based systems. [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS"), or [PC DOS](/wiki/IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS") when supplied by IBM, was designed to be similar to CP/M-80.[[18]](#cite_note-21) Each of these machines had a small boot program in ROM which loaded the OS itself from disk. The BIOS on the IBM-PC class machines was an extension of this idea and has accreted more features and functions in the 20 years since the first IBM-PC was introduced in 1981.

The most important of the early OSes on these machines was [Digital Research](/wiki/Digital_Research "Digital Research")'s [CP/M](/wiki/CP/M "CP/M")-80 for the 8080 / 8085 / Z80 CPUs. It was based on several Digital Equipment Corporation operating systems, mostly for the PDP-11 architecture. [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS"), or [PC DOS](/wiki/IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS") when supplied by IBM, was designed to be similar to CP/M-80.[[18]](#cite_note-21) Each of these machines had a small boot program in ROM which loaded the OS itself from disk. The BIOS on the IBM-PC class machines was an extension of this idea and has accreted more features and functions in the 20 years since the first IBM-PC was introduced in 1981.

The decreasing cost of display equipment and processors made it practical to provide graphical user interfaces for many operating systems, such as the generic [X Window System](/wiki/X_Window_System "X Window System") that is provided with many Unix systems, or other graphical systems such as [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Computer "Apple Computer")'s [classic Mac OS](/wiki/Classic_Mac_OS "Classic Mac OS") and [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS"), the [Radio Shack](/wiki/RadioShack "RadioShack") Color Computer's [OS-9 Level II/Multi-Vue](/wiki/OS-9 "OS-9"), [Commodore](/wiki/Commodore_International "Commodore International")'s [AmigaOS](/wiki/AmigaOS "AmigaOS"), [Atari TOS](/wiki/Atari_TOS "Atari TOS"), [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM")'s [OS/2](/wiki/OS/2 "OS/2"), and [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"). The original GUI was developed on the [Xerox Alto](/wiki/Xerox_Alto "Xerox Alto") computer system at Xerox [Palo Alto Research Center](/wiki/PARC_(company) "PARC (company)") in the early 1970s and commercialized by many vendors throughout the 1980s and 1990s.

Since the late 1990s, there have been three operating systems in widespread use on personal computers: [Apple Inc.](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")'s [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS"), the [open source](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software") [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux"), and [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"). Since 2005 and the [Mac transition to Intel processors](/wiki/Mac_transition_to_Intel_processors "Mac transition to Intel processors"), all have been developed mainly on the [x86](/wiki/X86 "X86") platform, although macOS retained [PowerPC](/wiki/PowerPC "PowerPC") support until 2009, and they have now [switched to Apple silicon](/wiki/Mac_transition_to_Apple_silicon "Mac transition to Apple silicon") and Linux remains ported to a multitude of architectures including ones such as [68k](/wiki/68k "68k"), [PA-RISC](/wiki/PA-RISC "PA-RISC"), and [DEC Alpha](/wiki/DEC_Alpha "DEC Alpha"), which have been long superseded and out of production, and [SPARC](/wiki/SPARC "SPARC") and [MIPS](/wiki/MIPS_architecture "MIPS architecture"), which are used in servers or embedded systems but no longer for desktop computers. Other operating systems such as AmigaOS and OS/2 remain in use, if at all, mainly by [retrocomputing](/wiki/Retrocomputing "Retrocomputing") enthusiasts or for specialized embedded applications.

title: History of operating systems
text:
[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Android_phone.jpg/250px-Android_phone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Android_phone.jpg)

[Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") is the most used [mobile operating system](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system").

In the early 1990s, [Psion](/wiki/Psion_(company) "Psion (company)") released the [Psion Series 3](/wiki/Psion_Series_3 "Psion Series 3") [PDA](/wiki/Personal_digital_assistant "Personal digital assistant"), a small mobile computing device. It supported user-written applications running on an operating system called [EPOC](/wiki/EPOC_(operating_system) "EPOC (operating system)"). Later versions of EPOC became [Symbian](/wiki/Symbian "Symbian"), an operating system used for mobile phones from [Nokia](/wiki/Nokia "Nokia"), [Ericsson](/wiki/Ericsson "Ericsson"), [Sony Ericsson](/wiki/Sony_Ericsson "Sony Ericsson"), [Motorola](/wiki/Motorola "Motorola"), [Samsung](/wiki/Samsung "Samsung") and phones developed for [NTT Docomo](/wiki/NTT_Docomo "NTT Docomo") by [Sharp](/wiki/Sharp_Corporation "Sharp Corporation"), [Fujitsu](/wiki/Fujitsu "Fujitsu") & [Mitsubishi](/wiki/Mitsubishi "Mitsubishi"). [Symbian](/wiki/Symbian "Symbian") was the world's most widely used smartphone operating system until 2010 with a peak market share of 74% in 2006. In 1996, [Palm Computing](/wiki/Palm,_Inc.#Founding_and_acquisition "Palm, Inc.") released the [Pilot 1000](/wiki/Pilot_1000 "Pilot 1000") and Pilot 5000, running [Palm OS](/wiki/Palm_OS "Palm OS"). Microsoft [Windows CE](/wiki/Windows_Embedded_Compact "Windows Embedded Compact") was the base for Pocket PC 2000, renamed [Windows Mobile](/wiki/Windows_Mobile "Windows Mobile") in 2003, which at its peak in 2007 was the most common operating system for smartphones in the U.S.

In the early 1990s, [Psion](/wiki/Psion_(company) "Psion (company)") released the [Psion Series 3](/wiki/Psion_Series_3 "Psion Series 3") [PDA](/wiki/Personal_digital_assistant "Personal digital assistant"), a small mobile computing device. It supported user-written applications running on an operating system called [EPOC](/wiki/EPOC_(operating_system) "EPOC (operating system)"). Later versions of EPOC became [Symbian](/wiki/Symbian "Symbian"), an operating system used for mobile phones from [Nokia](/wiki/Nokia "Nokia"), [Ericsson](/wiki/Ericsson "Ericsson"), [Sony Ericsson](/wiki/Sony_Ericsson "Sony Ericsson"), [Motorola](/wiki/Motorola "Motorola"), [Samsung](/wiki/Samsung "Samsung") and phones developed for [NTT Docomo](/wiki/NTT_Docomo "NTT Docomo") by [Sharp](/wiki/Sharp_Corporation "Sharp Corporation"), [Fujitsu](/wiki/Fujitsu "Fujitsu") & [Mitsubishi](/wiki/Mitsubishi "Mitsubishi"). [Symbian](/wiki/Symbian "Symbian") was the world's most widely used smartphone operating system until 2010 with a peak market share of 74% in 2006. In 1996, [Palm Computing](/wiki/Palm,_Inc.#Founding_and_acquisition "Palm, Inc.") released the [Pilot 1000](/wiki/Pilot_1000 "Pilot 1000") and Pilot 5000, running [Palm OS](/wiki/Palm_OS "Palm OS"). Microsoft [Windows CE](/wiki/Windows_Embedded_Compact "Windows Embedded Compact") was the base for Pocket PC 2000, renamed [Windows Mobile](/wiki/Windows_Mobile "Windows Mobile") in 2003, which at its peak in 2007 was the most common operating system for smartphones in the U.S.

In 2007, Apple introduced the [iPhone](/wiki/IPhone "IPhone") and its operating system, known as simply [iPhone OS](/wiki/IPhone_OS_1 "IPhone OS 1") (until the release of [iOS 4](/wiki/IOS_4 "IOS 4")), which, like [Mac OS X](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS"), is based on the [Unix-like](/wiki/Unix-like "Unix-like") [Darwin](/wiki/Darwin_(operating_system) "Darwin (operating system)"). In addition to these underpinnings, it also introduced a powerful and innovative graphic user interface that was later also used on the [tablet computer](/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer") [iPad](/wiki/IPad "IPad"). A year later, [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)"), with its own graphical user interface, was introduced, based on a modified [Linux kernel](/wiki/Linux_kernel "Linux kernel"), and [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") re-entered the mobile operating system market with [Windows Phone](/wiki/Windows_Phone "Windows Phone") in 2010, which was replaced by [Windows 10 Mobile](/wiki/Windows_10_Mobile "Windows 10 Mobile") in 2015.

In addition to these, a wide range of other [mobile operating systems](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system") are contending in this area.

title: History of operating systems
text:
## Rise of virtualization

Operating systems originally ran directly on the hardware itself and provided services to applications, but with virtualization, the operating system itself runs under the control of a [hypervisor](/wiki/Hypervisor "Hypervisor"), instead of being in direct control of the hardware.

On mainframes IBM introduced the notion of a [virtual machine](/wiki/Virtual_machine "Virtual machine") in 1968 with [CP/CMS](/wiki/CP/CMS "CP/CMS") on the [IBM System/360 Model 67](/wiki/IBM_System/360_Model_67 "IBM System/360 Model 67"), and extended this later in 1972 with [Virtual Machine Facility/370](/wiki/VM_(operating_system) "VM (operating system)") (VM/370) on [System/370](/wiki/IBM_System/370 "IBM System/370").

On [x86](/wiki/X86 "X86")-based [personal computers](/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer"), [VMware](/wiki/VMware "VMware") popularized this technology with their 1999 product, [VMware Workstation](/wiki/VMware_Workstation "VMware Workstation"),[[19]](#cite_note-22) and their 2001 VMware GSX Server and VMware ESX Server products.[[20]](#cite_note-23) Later, a wide range of products from others, including [Xen](/wiki/Xen "Xen"), [KVM](/wiki/Kernel-based_Virtual_Machine "Kernel-based Virtual Machine") and [Hyper-V](/wiki/Hyper-V "Hyper-V") meant that by 2010 it was reported that more than 80 percent of enterprises had a virtualization program or project in place, and that 25 percent of all server workloads would be in a virtual machine.[[21]](#cite_note-24)

Over time, the line between virtual machines, monitors, and operating systems was blurred:
breadcrumb: Category:Operating systems > History of operating systems

title: History of operating systems
text:
- Hypervisors grew more complex, gaining their own application programming interface,[[22]](#cite_note-25) memory management or file system.[[23]](#cite_note-26)
- Virtualization becomes a key feature of operating systems, as exemplified by [KVM](/wiki/Kernel-based_Virtual_Machine "Kernel-based Virtual Machine") and [LXC](/wiki/LXC "LXC") in Linux, [Hyper-V](/wiki/Hyper-V "Hyper-V") in [Windows Server 2008](/wiki/Windows_Server_2008 "Windows Server 2008") or [HP Integrity Virtual Machines](/wiki/HP_Integrity_Virtual_Machines "HP Integrity Virtual Machines") in [HP-UX](/wiki/HP-UX "HP-UX").
- In some systems, such as [POWER5](/wiki/POWER5 "POWER5") and later POWER servers from IBM, the hypervisor is no longer optional.[[24]](#cite_note-27)
- Radically simplified operating systems, such as [CoreOS](/wiki/CoreOS "CoreOS") have been designed to run only on virtual systems.[[25]](#cite_note-28)
- Applications have been re-designed to run directly on a virtual machine monitor.[[26]](#cite_note-29)

In many ways, virtual machine software today plays the role formerly held by the operating system, including managing the hardware resources (processor, memory, I/O devices), applying scheduling policies, or allowing system administrators to manage the system.

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text: **Comparison of user features of operating systems** refers to a comparison of the general user features of major [operating systems](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") in a narrative format. It does not encompass a full exhaustive comparison or description of all technical details of all operating systems. It is a comparison of basic roles and the most prominent features. It also includes the most important features of the operating system's origins, historical development, and role.

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text:
## Overview

Main article: [Operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system")

An operating system (OS) is [system software](/wiki/System_software "System software") that manages computer hardware, [software](/wiki/Computer_software "Computer software") resources, and provides common [services](/wiki/Daemon_(computing) "Daemon (computing)") for computer programs.

[Time-sharing](/wiki/Time-sharing "Time-sharing") operating systems [schedule tasks](/wiki/Scheduler_(computing) "Scheduler (computing)") for efficient use of the system and may also include accounting software for cost allocation of [processor time](/wiki/Scheduling_(computing) "Scheduling (computing)"), [mass storage](/wiki/Mass_storage "Mass storage"), printing, and other resources.

For hardware functions such as [input and output](/wiki/Input_and_output "Input and output") and [memory allocation](/wiki/Memory_allocation "Memory allocation"), the operating system acts as an intermediary between programs and the computer hardware,[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) although the application code is usually executed directly by the hardware and frequently makes [system calls](/wiki/System_call "System call") to an OS function or is [interrupted](/wiki/Interrupt "Interrupt") by it. Operating systems are found on many devices that contain a computer – from cellular phones and video game consoles to [web servers](/wiki/Web_server "Web server") and [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer").

Operating systems are found on many devices that contain a computer – from cellular phones and video game consoles to [web servers](/wiki/Web_server "Web server") and [supercomputers](/wiki/Supercomputer "Supercomputer").

As of June 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Comparison_of_user_features_of_operating_systems&action=edit), the dominant general-purpose desktop operating system is [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") with a market share of around 72.91%. [macOS](/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") by [Apple Inc.](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") is in second place (14.93%), and the varieties of [Linux](/wiki/Linux "Linux") are collectively in third place (4.04%).[[3]](#cite_note-statcounter-desktop-3) In the [mobile](/wiki/Mobile_operating_system "Mobile operating system") sector, including both smartphones and [tablets](/wiki/Tablet_computer "Tablet computer"), [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") is dominant with a market share of 71%, followed by Apple's [iOS](/wiki/IOS "IOS") with 28%;[[4]](#cite_note-statcounter-mobile-and-tablet-4) for smartphones alone, Android has 72% and iOS has 28%.[[5]](#cite_note-5) [Linux distributions](/wiki/Linux_distribution "Linux distribution") are dominant in the server and supercomputing sectors. Other specialized classes of operating systems (special-purpose operating systems)[[6]](#cite_note-auto-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)), such as [embedded](/wiki/Embedded_system "Embedded system") and real-time systems, exist for many applications. [Security-focused operating systems](/wiki/Security-focused_operating_system "Security-focused operating system") also exist. Some operating systems have low system requirements (i.e. [light-weight Linux distribution](/wiki/Light-weight_Linux_distribution "Light-weight Linux distribution")). Others may have higher system requirements.

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text:
### Overview

[MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") (acronym for Microsoft Disk Operating System) is an operating system for [x86](/wiki/X86 "X86")-based personal computers mostly developed by [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"). Collectively, MS-DOS, its rebranding as [IBM PC DOS](/wiki/IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS"), and some operating systems attempting to be compatible with MS-DOS, are sometimes referred to as "DOS" (which is also the generic acronym for [disk operating system](/wiki/Disk_operating_system "Disk operating system")). MS-DOS was the main operating system for [IBM PC compatible](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") personal computers during the 1980s, from which point it was gradually superseded by operating systems offering a [graphical user interface](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") (GUI), in various generations of the graphical Microsoft Windows operating system.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

IBM licensed and re-released it in 1981 as [PC DOS](/wiki/PC_DOS "PC DOS") 1.0 for use in its PCs. Although MS-DOS and PC DOS were initially developed in parallel by Microsoft and IBM, the two products diverged after twelve years, in 1993, with recognizable differences in compatibility, syntax, and capabilities.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text:
IBM licensed and re-released it in 1981 as [PC DOS](/wiki/PC_DOS "PC DOS") 1.0 for use in its PCs. Although MS-DOS and PC DOS were initially developed in parallel by Microsoft and IBM, the two products diverged after twelve years, in 1993, with recognizable differences in compatibility, syntax, and capabilities.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

During its lifetime, [several competing products](/wiki/Comparison_of_DOS_operating_systems "Comparison of DOS operating systems") were released for the x86 platform,[[8]](#cite_note-roy-8) and MS-DOS went through eight versions, until development ceased in 2000.[[9]](#cite_note-Historical_Essays-9) Initially, MS-DOS was targeted at [Intel 8086](/wiki/Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") processors running on computer hardware using [floppy disks](/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk") to store and access not only the operating system, but application software and user data as well. Progressive version releases delivered support for other mass storage media in ever greater sizes and formats, along with added feature support for newer processors and rapidly evolving computer architectures. Ultimately, it was the key product in Microsoft's development from a [programming language](/wiki/Programming_language "Programming language") company to a diverse software development firm, providing the company with essential revenue and marketing resources. It was also the underlying basic operating system on which early versions of Windows ran as a GUI.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text:
### Overview

Microsoft Windows, commonly referred to as Windows, is a group of several [proprietary](/wiki/Proprietary_software "Proprietary software") [graphical](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") operating system families, all of which are developed and marketed by [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"). Each family caters to a certain sector of the computing industry. Active Microsoft Windows families include [Windows NT](/wiki/Windows_NT "Windows NT") and [Windows IoT](/wiki/Windows_IoT "Windows IoT"); these may encompass subfamilies, (e.g. [Windows Server](/wiki/Windows_Server "Windows Server") or [Windows Embedded Compact](/wiki/Windows_Embedded_Compact "Windows Embedded Compact")) (Windows CE). Defunct Microsoft Windows families include [Windows 9x](/wiki/Windows_9x "Windows 9x"), [Windows Mobile](/wiki/Windows_Mobile "Windows Mobile"), and [Windows Phone](/wiki/Windows_Phone "Windows Phone").

Microsoft Windows, commonly referred to as Windows, is a group of several [proprietary](/wiki/Proprietary_software "Proprietary software") [graphical](/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface") operating system families, all of which are developed and marketed by [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"). Each family caters to a certain sector of the computing industry. Active Microsoft Windows families include [Windows NT](/wiki/Windows_NT "Windows NT") and [Windows IoT](/wiki/Windows_IoT "Windows IoT"); these may encompass subfamilies, (e.g. [Windows Server](/wiki/Windows_Server "Windows Server") or [Windows Embedded Compact](/wiki/Windows_Embedded_Compact "Windows Embedded Compact")) (Windows CE). Defunct Microsoft Windows families include [Windows 9x](/wiki/Windows_9x "Windows 9x"), [Windows Mobile](/wiki/Windows_Mobile "Windows Mobile"), and [Windows Phone](/wiki/Windows_Phone "Windows Phone").

Microsoft announced an [operating environment](/wiki/Operating_environment "Operating environment") named *Windows* on 10 November 1983, as a graphical [operating system shell](/wiki/Shell_(computing) "Shell (computing)") for [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") in response to the growing interest in graphical user interfaces (GUIs); Windows 1.0 first shipped on 20 November 1985.[[10]](#cite_note-aboutcomnov-10) Microsoft Windows came to [dominate](/wiki/Dominance_(economics) "Dominance (economics)") the world's personal computer (PC) market with [over 90% market share](/wiki/Usage_share_of_operating_systems "Usage share of operating systems"), overtaking [Mac OS](/wiki/Classic_Mac_OS "Classic Mac OS"), which had been introduced in 1984, while Microsoft has in 2020 lost its dominance of the consumer operating system market, with Windows down to 30%, lower than [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc "Apple Inc")'s 31% mobile-only share (65% for desktop operating systems only, i.e. "[PCs](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible")" vs. Apple's 28% desktop share) in its home market, the US, and 32% globally (77% for desktops), where Google's Android leads.

Microsoft announced an [operating environment](/wiki/Operating_environment "Operating environment") named *Windows* on 10 November 1983, as a graphical [operating system shell](/wiki/Shell_(computing) "Shell (computing)") for [MS-DOS](/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS") in response to the growing interest in graphical user interfaces (GUIs); Windows 1.0 first shipped on 20 November 1985.[[10]](#cite_note-aboutcomnov-10) Microsoft Windows came to [dominate](/wiki/Dominance_(economics) "Dominance (economics)") the world's personal computer (PC) market with [over 90% market share](/wiki/Usage_share_of_operating_systems "Usage share of operating systems"), overtaking [Mac OS](/wiki/Classic_Mac_OS "Classic Mac OS"), which had been introduced in 1984, while Microsoft has in 2020 lost its dominance of the consumer operating system market, with Windows down to 30%, lower than [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc "Apple Inc")'s 31% mobile-only share (65% for desktop operating systems only, i.e. "[PCs](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible")" vs. Apple's 28% desktop share) in its home market, the US, and 32% globally (77% for desktops), where Google's Android leads.

Apple came to see Windows as an unfair encroachment on their innovation in GUI development as implemented on products such as the [Lisa](/wiki/Apple_Lisa "Apple Lisa") and [Macintosh](/wiki/Macintosh "Macintosh") (eventually settled in court in Microsoft's favor in 1993). As of January 2023[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Comparison_of_user_features_of_operating_systems&action=edit), on PCs, Windows is still the most popular operating system in all countries.[[11]](#cite_note-statcounter-os-11)[[3]](#cite_note-statcounter-desktop-3) However, in 2014, Microsoft admitted losing the majority of the overall operating system market to [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)"),[[12]](#cite_note-12) because of the massive growth in sales of Android [smartphones](/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone"). In 2014, the number of Windows devices sold was less than 25% that of Android devices sold. This comparison, however, may not be fully relevant, as the two operating systems traditionally target different platforms. Still, numbers for server use of Windows (that are comparable to competitors) show one third market share, similar to that for end user use.

The most recent version for [server computers](/wiki/Server_(computing) "Server (computing)") is [Windows Server](/wiki/Windows_Server "Windows Server"), version 20H2.[[13]](#cite_note-13) [A specialized version of Windows](/wiki/Xbox_One_system_software "Xbox One system software") also runs on the [Xbox One](/wiki/Xbox_One "Xbox One") [video game console](/wiki/Video_game_console "Video game console").[[14]](#cite_note-14)

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text:
### Windows 95

[Windows 95](/wiki/Windows_95 "Windows 95") introduced a redesigned [shell](/wiki/Windows_shell "Windows shell") based around a [desktop metaphor](/wiki/Desktop_metaphor "Desktop metaphor"); [File shortcuts](/wiki/Shortcut_(computing)#Microsoft_Windows "Shortcut (computing)") (also known as shell links) were introduced[[15]](#cite_note-WinLNK-15) and the desktop was re-purposed to hold shortcuts to applications, files and folders, reminiscent of Mac OS.

In [Windows 3.1](/wiki/Windows_3.1 "Windows 3.1") the desktop was used to display icons of running applications. In Windows 95, the currently running applications were displayed as buttons on a [taskbar](/wiki/Taskbar "Taskbar") across the bottom of the screen.[[16]](#cite_note-16) The taskbar also contained a notification area used to display icons for background applications, a volume control and the current time.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

The [Start menu](/wiki/Start_menu "Start menu"), invoked by clicking the "Start" button on the taskbar or by pressing the [Windows key](/wiki/Windows_key "Windows key"), was introduced as an additional means of launching applications or opening documents. While maintaining the program groups used by its predecessor [Program Manager](/wiki/Program_Manager "Program Manager"), it also displayed applications within cascading sub-menus.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

title: Comparison of user features of operating systems
text:
The [Start menu](/wiki/Start_menu "Start menu"), invoked by clicking the "Start" button on the taskbar or by pressing the [Windows key](/wiki/Windows_key "Windows key"), was introduced as an additional means of launching applications or opening documents. While maintaining the program groups used by its predecessor [Program Manager](/wiki/Program_Manager "Program Manager"), it also displayed applications within cascading sub-menus.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

The previous [File Manager](/wiki/File_Manager_(Windows) "File Manager (Windows)") program was replaced by [Windows Explorer](/wiki/Windows_Explorer "Windows Explorer") and the Explorer-based [Control Panel](/wiki/Control_Panel_(Windows) "Control Panel (Windows)") and several other [special folders](/wiki/Special_folder "Special folder") were added such as My Computer, Dial Up Networking, Recycle Bin, Network Neighborhood, My Documents, Recent documents, Fonts, Printers, and [My Briefcase](/wiki/Briefcase_(Microsoft_Windows) "Briefcase (Microsoft Windows)") among others. [AutoRun](/wiki/AutoRun "AutoRun") was introduced for CD drives.

The user interface looked dramatically different from prior versions of Windows, but its design language did not have a special name like *[Metro](/wiki/Metro_(design_language) "Metro (design language)")*, *[Aqua](/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface) "Aqua (user interface)")* or *[Material Design](/wiki/Material_Design "Material Design")*. Internally it was called "the new shell" and later simply "the shell".[[19]](#cite_note-19) The subproject within Microsoft to develop the new shell was internally known as "Stimpy".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Internally it was called "the new shell" and later simply "the shell".[[19]](#cite_note-19) The subproject within Microsoft to develop the new shell was internally known as "Stimpy".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In 1994, Microsoft designers [Mark Malamud](/wiki/Mark_Malamud "Mark Malamud") and Erik Gavriluk approached [Brian Eno](/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno") to compose music for the Windows 95 project.[[21]](#cite_note-21) The result was the six-second start-up music-sound of the Windows 95 operating system, *[The Microsoft Sound](/wiki/The_Microsoft_Sound "The Microsoft Sound")* and it was first released as a startup sound in May 1995 on Windows 95 May Test Release build 468.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

When released for Windows 95 and Windows NT 4.0, [Internet Explorer 4](/wiki/Internet_Explorer_4 "Internet Explorer 4") came with an optional [Windows Desktop Update](/wiki/Windows_Desktop_Update "Windows Desktop Update"), which modified the shell to provide several additional updates to Windows Explorer, including a *Quick Launch* toolbar, and new features integrated with Internet Explorer, such as [Active Desktop](/wiki/Active_Desktop "Active Desktop") (which allowed Internet content to be displayed directly on the desktop).

When released for Windows 95 and Windows NT 4.0, [Internet Explorer 4](/wiki/Internet_Explorer_4 "Internet Explorer 4") came with an optional [Windows Desktop Update](/wiki/Windows_Desktop_Update "Windows Desktop Update"), which modified the shell to provide several additional updates to Windows Explorer, including a *Quick Launch* toolbar, and new features integrated with Internet Explorer, such as [Active Desktop](/wiki/Active_Desktop "Active Desktop") (which allowed Internet content to be displayed directly on the desktop).

Some of the user interface elements introduced in Windows 95, such as the desktop, taskbar, Start menu and Windows Explorer file manager, remained fundamentally unchanged on future versions of Windows.

text:
### Windows 10

A new iteration of the [Start menu](/wiki/Start_menu "Start menu") is used on the [Windows 10](/wiki/Windows_10 "Windows 10") desktop, with a list of places and other options on the left side, and tiles representing applications on the right. The menu can be resized, and expanded into a full-screen display, which is the default option in Tablet mode.[[23]](#cite_note-tomsguide-unveiled-23) A new virtual desktop system was added. A feature known as Task View displays all open windows and allows users to switch between them, or switch between multiple workspaces.[[23]](#cite_note-tomsguide-unveiled-23) Universal apps, which previously could be used only in full screen mode, can now be used in self-contained windows similarly to other programs.[[24]](#cite_note-verge-win10-24)[[23]](#cite_note-tomsguide-unveiled-23) Program windows can now be snapped to quadrants of the screen by dragging them to the corner. When a window is snapped to one side of the screen, Task View appears and the user is prompted to choose a second window to fill the unused side of the screen (called "Snap Assist").[[23]](#cite_note-tomsguide-unveiled-23) Windows' system icons were also changed.[[25]](#cite_note-verge-closerlook-25)

It is accessed by clicking an icon in the notification area, or dragging from the right of the screen. Notifications can be synced between multiple devices.[[24]](#cite_note-verge-win10-24)[[25]](#cite_note-verge-closerlook-25) The Settings app (formerly PC Settings) was refreshed and now includes more options that were previously exclusive to the desktop [Control Panel](/wiki/Control_Panel_(Windows) "Control Panel (Windows)").[[26]](#cite_note-pcpro-settingsmenu-26)[[27]](#cite_note-cnet-settingsmenu-27)

It is accessed by clicking an icon in the notification area, or dragging from the right of the screen. Notifications can be synced between multiple devices.[[24]](#cite_note-verge-win10-24)[[25]](#cite_note-verge-closerlook-25) The Settings app (formerly PC Settings) was refreshed and now includes more options that were previously exclusive to the desktop [Control Panel](/wiki/Control_Panel_(Windows) "Control Panel (Windows)").[[26]](#cite_note-pcpro-settingsmenu-26)[[27]](#cite_note-cnet-settingsmenu-27)

Windows 10 is designed to adapt its user interface based on the type of device being used and available input methods. It offers two separate user interface modes: a user interface optimized for mouse and keyboard, and a "Tablet mode" designed for touchscreens. Users can toggle between these two modes at any time, and Windows can prompt or automatically switch when certain events occur, such as disabling Tablet mode on a tablet if a keyboard or mouse is plugged in, or when a [2-in-1 PC](/wiki/2-in-1_PC "2-in-1 PC") is switched to its laptop state. In Tablet mode, programs default to a maximized view, and the taskbar contains a back button and hides buttons for opened or pinned programs by default; Task View is used instead to switch between programs. The full screen Start menu is used in this mode, similarly to Windows 8, but scrolls vertically instead of horizontally.[[28]](#cite_note-verge-continuum-28)[[29]](#cite_note-thurrotcom-tablet1-29)[[30]](#cite_note-thurrotcom-tablet2-30)[[31]](#cite_note-winbeta-w10touch-31)

#### Overview

The classic Mac OS [[a]](#cite_note-32) (**System Software**) is the series of operating systems developed for the [Macintosh](/wiki/Macintosh "Macintosh") family of personal computers by Apple Inc. from 1984 to 2001, starting with [System 1](/wiki/System_1 "System 1") and ending with [Mac OS 9](/wiki/Mac_OS_9 "Mac OS 9"). The Macintosh operating system is credited with having popularized the graphical user interface concept.[[32]](#cite_note-33) It was included with every Macintosh that was sold during the era in which it was developed, and many updates to the system software were done in conjunction with the introduction of new Macintosh systems.
